topic: Tiny fast ball detection and tracking in sports video (TrackNet family, heatmap detectors, multi-frame input, few-label training)

findings.method: TrackNet (original): heatmap-based CNN that takes 640x360 input, a single frame or several consecutive frames, and outputs a per-pixel ball-location heatmap. Designed for tiny, fast balls in tennis/badminton broadcast video.
findings.how_it_applies: Multi-frame input plus heatmap output is the design that addresses small, fast balls. Robo Scout's ~10 px Pollen/Nectar balls at 60 fps fit this regime better than single-frame YOLO boxes. Heatmap peaks also give sub-box localization and a natural way to emit missing-ball (no peak) frames for trajectory gaps.
findings.evidence: arXiv:1907.03698, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.03698 (reports F1 98.5 on a main tennis video, precision 95.3 / recall 75.7 on 10-fold cross-validation over partially labeled videos; the page gives no label or frame counts; no badminton numbers on the abstract page)

findings.method: TrackNetV4: adds learnable motion-attention maps built from frame differencing, fused with visual features through a motion-aware fusion module. Plug-and-play into TrackNetV2/V3-style heatmap trackers.
findings.how_it_applies: Explicit motion cues help separate the ball from static robots, the score overlay and the Hive Cell structure, reducing false positives on small similar blobs. This is a drop-in addition to a heatmap model and can reuse the existing frame-difference scanner signal.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2409.14543, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14543 and project page https://tracknetv4.github.io (abstract and project page only; no numeric tables were retrieved)

findings.method: TrackNetV5: replaces V4's absolute frame differences with signed motion-polarity fields (Motion Direction Decoupling) and adds a Transformer residual spatio-temporal refinement head aimed at recovering occluded or missed targets. Reported F1 0.9859 and accuracy 0.9733 on the TrackNetV2 dataset with about 3.7% more FLOPs than V4.
findings.how_it_applies: Signed motion direction helps distinguish a ball rising into the Hive Cell from one falling or from a static robot part, which matters for the entry/no-entry question. The residual refinement is a direct answer to the 'ball path lost mid-air' problem: it fills short gaps where the ball is occluded or invisible.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2512.02789, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02789 (abstract only; the training recipe and per-dataset ablations were not retrieved)

findings.method: WASB-SBDT (Widely Applicable Strong Baseline for Sports Ball Detection and Tracking): high-resolution feature extraction, position-aware training, and temporal-consistency inference. Reports AP gains of 7.8 to 16.8% over six prior SBDT methods on five datasets across sports, and ships open-source code and datasets.
findings.how_it_applies: A cross-sport, pretrained-style baseline that generalizes beyond one court. Its high-resolution training and temporal-consistency post-processing are the parts most transferable to Robo Scout, and the repo gives a ready benchmark to compare the current YOLO26 ball detector against on the 20 labeled videos before committing to a rewrite. Note the paper says it is not the fastest method.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2311.05237, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05237 (BMVC 2023); code https://github.com/nttcom/WASB-SBDT

findings.method: SAHI (Slicing Aided Hyper Inference): run the detector on overlapping tiles of the full frame (plus optional full-frame pass) to raise small-object recall; reported AP gains of roughly 5-7 points from inference alone on VisDrone/xView and more with slicing-aware fine-tuning.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's 10 px balls at 1280x720 are below the stride-level resolution of a standard YOLO input. Tiling the frame (or a Hive Cell ROI at higher effective resolution) is a training-free way to improve recall that works directly with the existing YOLO26 ball model, at a compute cost roughly proportional to tile count. It is not sports-specific and was not validated on ball sports in the sources found.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2202.06934, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06934 (SAHI paper; gains reported on VisDrone and xView, aerial data)

findings.method: Semi-supervised / pseudo-label training for ball detection from few labels: a teacher detector produces pseudo-labels on unlabeled broadcast frames to train a student, with a small labeled seed set (soccer player and ball detection).
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout has about 20 labeled matches with per-launch reviews. Pseudo-labeling unlabeled frames from the held-out-style broadcast, with the current detector as teacher and confidence filtering, could expand the ball training set without new annotation. The sports-specific results found are for soccer, not tiny 10 px balls, so gains on Robo Scout must be measured.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2204.06859, https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.06859 (Vandeghen et al., CVsports 2022); a tennis progressive semi-supervised framework in IEEE Access Jan 2024 (https://doaj.org/article/a55638e525d3468ab5206dd6593dae71) was found but not read in full

findings.method: Motion/temporal cues for tiny-ball gating: frame-difference and polarity signals together with an explicit track state (predict through gaps, reacquire) rather than per-frame detection alone.
findings.how_it_applies: Addresses the finding that only one Hive entry is found because balls are lost mid-air. A tracker that keeps a constant-velocity or learned-motion state through short detection gaps, with the heatmap/motion model re-detecting, gives continuous paths for the entry classifier. This ties to TrackNetV5's refinement head conceptually; the specific gap-filling parameters were not retrieved.
findings.evidence: Derived from arXiv:2512.02789 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02789) and arXiv:2409.14543 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14543); the concrete tracker design is an inference, not a sourced recipe

recommendation: Replace the single-frame YOLO ball detector with a multi-frame heatmap tracker in the TrackNet lineage (start with TrackNetV4's motion-attention fusion on top of the TrackNet heatmap design, or TrackNetV5 if its code is available), trained at the native 1280x720 resolution or on Hive-Cell ROI crops for effective resolution. First benchmark the existing YOLO26 ball detector against WASB-SBDT (https://github.com/nttcom/WASB-SBDT) on the 20 labeled videos, and add SAHI-style tiling as a cheap recall boost while the heatmap model is built. Expand training labels by pseudo-labeling unlabeled frames with the current teacher. Keep a gap-tolerant track state so Hive entries are not lost mid-air. Caveat: TrackNetV5 and V4 numbers come from abstracts only, and no source found reports 10 px balls at 60 fps directly, so validate on the 20 labeled videos before relying on any reported gain.

topic: Basketball made/missed shot detection from a fixed camera: hoop-region analysis, ball-in-hoop classification, open-source projects and accuracy

findings.method: Rule-based ball-in-hoop outcome from ball motion near the rim (Roboflow shot evaluator)
findings.how_it_applies: When the ball disappears near the rim (occluded by the net), decide make vs miss from its vertical speed relative to freefall: 10-90% of freefall = made (net drag), 100% = airball passing behind rim, 0% = stationary ball rejected. Robo Scout's Hive Cell is the analogue of the rim, but balls rise from below into the cell in this view, so the sign and reference frame must be reversed; the speed-ratio idea still transfers. Also tags ambiguous cases (occluded, rattled) instead of forcing a label, which fits the 'only 1 of many entries found' problem: report uncertainty rather than dropping the event.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched; blog.roboflow.com URL redirects here); code: https://github.com/aarnavshah12/shot-tracker (linked from the article, not fetched directly)

findings.method: Occlusion-tolerant tracking with a release-to-rim trajectory state machine (Roboflow shot evaluator)
findings.how_it_applies: The article defines a shot start as ball separation from the shooter's wrist while moving upward, then requires the projected arc to point toward the rim box or the attempt is discarded. It keeps a stateful engine across frames (positions, velocities, detection confidence). This is a direct fix for Robo Scout's mid-air track loss: keep a per-shot state from launch to Cell entry, allow gaps, and link the launch event to the outcome event instead of re-detecting each frame. Its reported failure mode (net hides ball for 2 frames, two makes logged as misses) is exactly the risk Robo Scout faces, so gap tolerance must be tuned explicitly.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched)

findings.method: RF-DETR small detector for ball and rim, trained on a fork of a public shooting dataset (~9.8k images)
findings.how_it_applies: Reported ball/rim detector metrics are mAP50 88.84, precision 75.7, recall 84.9, with the ball detected in 98.1% of in-flight frames (759/774). These are the only concrete detection-accuracy numbers found for a basketball shot pipeline. Robo Scout's YOLO26 ball detector is a similar setup; the benchmark gives a reference for what a single-camera ball/rim detector achieves, and the gap to 98% in-flight recall is a target to measure against. Dataset: University of Arizona 'Basketball Shooting Robot' (named in the article; not fetched).
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched)

findings.method: Faster R-CNN ball and rim detector with a per-shot make/miss README (anishcd/basketball-shot-detection)
findings.how_it_applies: Two-class detector (Basketball, Rim) with Faster R-CNN ResNet-50 FPN, trained with SGD. The README says it classifies makes and misses, but the fetched page does not show the decision logic and reports no accuracy, precision, recall or mAP. Use only as a baseline for a two-class rim+ball detector; do not rely on its make/miss claim.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/anishcd/basketball-shot-detection (fetched); license not stated on page

findings.method: Trajectory curve fit plus hoop overlay (chonyy/basketball-shot-detection)
findings.how_it_applies: Page shows color-coded outcomes (orange hoop, blue ball, purple undetermined, red miss, green make) and trajectory-fit figures, suggesting a curve is fit to tracked ball points and compared with the hoop. The page does not state the comparison rule or any accuracy number. The approach (fit a parabola to the launch-to-hoop track, extrapolate whether it crosses the hoop opening) is useful for Robo Scout's trajectory features, but the source gives no evidence it works.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/chonyy/basketball-shot-detection (fetched; no LICENSE visible in the listing)

findings.method: Patent-described hoop ROI with background subtraction (net motion as make signal)
findings.how_it_applies: Patents describe a hoop ROI enclosing the rim, with motion in that region (via background subtraction such as MOG, or a CNN) used as a make/miss signal, and Tiny YOLO for shooter foot position. Net-motion detection is a classical cue that does not depend on the ball being visible; it could complement the Cell-tip signal (the Cell tipping is ground truth for entry). Patent claims are not validated accuracy; treat as idea sources only.
findings.evidence: Search result snippets from https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11400355 and https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11594029 (snippets only, not fetched)

findings.method: Accuracy gap: no open-source made/missed accuracy benchmark found
findings.how_it_applies: Searches found no peer-reviewed or public benchmark reporting made/missed accuracy from a fixed side camera. The NCAA event-recognition paper (arXiv 2007.06288) reports 0.887 success/failure activity performance at threshold 0.7, but this is an activity-level metric on a different task. Robo Scout should build its own evaluation on its ~20 labeled matches (per-launch and per-entry labels) rather than trust any external number.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.06288 (search snippet only, not fetched)

recommendation: Replace per-frame hoop-entry detection with a per-shot state machine: link each launch (wrist separation plus upward velocity, arc projected toward the Cell box) to an outcome, allow occlusion gaps, and decide entry from the ball's speed and position near the Cell (the Roboflow drop-speed rule, with direction reversed for balls rising from below), plus a tipping-based ground-truth check. Tag ambiguous shots instead of dropping them. Use the Roboflow reference numbers (ball recall about 98% in flight) as a target, and measure against Robo Scout's own labeled matches because no external made/missed accuracy benchmark was found.

topic: Counting objects entering a container or goal region from video (made-basket counters, bin-entry counting): ROI state machines, persistence-based confirmation, occlusion by rim/frame

findings.method: Per-track LineZone-style crossing with persistence confirmation: a side change is counted only after the new side is held for minimum_crossing_threshold consecutive observations, and per-track side history is dropped only after max_absent_frames (default max(30, threshold+1)).
findings.how_it_applies: Replace per-frame 'ball inside Hive Cell box' tests with a per-track state (outside / inside-candidate / inside-confirmed). Require N consecutive frames inside the Cell ROI (or across its rim plane) before counting an entry, which suppresses single-frame detector flicker. Keep the track's state alive for a max-absent window so a ball that vanishes behind the rim or net for a few frames is not reset to a new, uncounted track. Negative or unconfirmed track IDs must never be counted, which matters given the identity-swap problem.
findings.evidence: https://supervision.roboflow.com/latest/detection/tools/line_zone/ (LineZone.trigger: minimum_crossing_threshold, per-track side history, max_absent_frames, negative tracker_id never counted)

findings.method: PolygonZone entry counting via a seen-set of tracker IDs: zone.trigger(detections) gives per-frame in-zone masks and current_count is the instantaneous count; entries are counted by keeping a set of tracker_ids first observed inside the zone.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout can count a Cell entry once per ball track by adding the track ID to a set on first confirmed in-zone observation, and attribute it to the launching robot via the launch-to-track association instead of the current robot track ID, which avoids the identity-swap error at the moment of entry. Note that current_count alone undercounts because balls settle and leave the zone.
findings.evidence: https://supervision.roboflow.com/0.29.0/how_to/count_in_zone/ and https://blog.roboflow.com/how-to-count-objects-in-a-zone (search snippets only, not fetched in full)

findings.method: Made-basket state machine with trajectory fitting and occlusion disambiguation by drop-speed relative to freefall: the ball is detected in flight, a release is logged only when the ball separates upward from the shooter, a parabola is fitted and projected toward the rim box, and when the ball reappears after being hidden, its vertical speed relative to freefall (10 to 90 percent = net make, 100 percent = behind-rim miss, 0 = stationary/rejected) decides the outcome. Ambiguous cases are tagged 'occluded' or 'rattled' rather than guessed.
findings.how_it_applies: Directly targets Robo Scout's lost-mid-air problem: a ball that rises into the Cell from below and disappears behind the Cell edge can be resolved by fitting a parabola to the pre-occlusion track, projecting it, and checking the re-acquired ball's motion against freefall or settling behavior. Tagging ambiguous events as 'occluded' gives a per-shot confidence field and avoids silent misses. Porting this needs the Cell's pixel rim box and a pixels-per-meter scale, which the article derives from rim width.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched; redirect from blog.roboflow.com). Code: https://github.com/aarnavshah12/shot-tracker (repo linked from article, not opened)

findings.method: Dual-evidence confirmation: count an entry only when the ball is seen entering the Cell and is then not seen exiting it, or when a settled ball is detected inside the Cell box; treat front-rim bounce-outs as a separate state (rattled miss) using a bounce-near-hoop pause.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's Cell is a container whose balls settle inside, so 'ball appears inside and stays' is a strong positive even when the in-flight track is broken. Pausing the state machine during rim bounces avoids double-counting or false misses from bounce-outs.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched, 'rattled make/miss' and bounce pause described)

findings.method: Failure-mode reference: the same article reports that two genuine makes were recorded as misses because the net hid the ball for two frames, and that pump fakes triggered false launches until a wrist-separation rule was added.
findings.how_it_applies: Expect a few-frame occlusion to be the main source of missed Cell entries; the Robo Scout counter needs an occlusion grace window and a launch-onset rule (ball separating from robot/launcher region moving upward) to avoid false shots.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-basketball-shot-evaluator (fetched)

findings.method: Zone-based patent approaches (attempt zone, make zone, entry/exit states; ROI split into 9 zones; background-subtraction net check).
findings.how_it_applies: Supports a design where the Cell is split into an entry band (just above the rim), an inside band, and an exit band, and entries are confirmed by the ordered sequence entry-then-inside. Background subtraction (MOG) on the Cell interior can serve as a cheap settle/occupancy signal that does not depend on the ball detector.
findings.evidence: US patents found via search: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11594029 and https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10489656 (search snippets only, claims not read in full)

recommendation: Rebuild the Hive Cell counter as a per-track ROI state machine (outside, candidate-inside, confirmed-inside) with an N-frame persistence threshold and a max-absent grace window so that tracks lost behind the rim are kept alive instead of reset, and count each track ID at most once. Attribute each entry to the robot via the launch association captured at launch time, not the current identity-swapping robot track. Add the parabolic-arc projection plus drop-speed-vs-freefall rule from the shot-tracker article to resolve occluded in-flight balls, and add a settled-ball-inside-Cell check as a second positive signal. Note that the shot-tracker repo and the NYU repo were not opened, and the patents were checked from search snippets only.

topic: Attributing a projectile to its source robot/player: backtracking ball trajectories to the launch point, parabolic fitting, linking release to the nearest tracked agent (sports analytics "who shot/passed the ball")

findings.method: Physics-constrained parabola fit per flight segment, then backtrack to the launch point and time (Tracker-style workflow: fit x(t), y(t) and read launch velocity/angle from coefficients, with the origin fixed at the launch point)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout loses balls mid-air, so fit short ballistic segments (x = x0 + vx*t, y = y0 + vy*t - g*t^2/2 in image coordinates with a known scale) on each confident run of ball detections. Solve for launch time and position by back-projecting to where the ball leaves the robot's bounding box. Use the fitted launch point, not the last-seen track position, to attribute the shot. Parabola fitting is the simplest constrained model and tolerates the 10 px Pollen ball's noisy centroids better than free-form smoothing.
findings.evidence: Tracker/projectile-motion fitting workflows, e.g. Parabolic Trajectory of a Basketball Shot video study (https://www.fizziq.org/en/activities/basketball/); Tracker pedagogical paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.6489); Glossary: y = x*tan(a) - g*x^2/(2*v0^2*cos^2(a)) approximation for short trajectories (https://www.fizziq.org/en/glossary/parabolic-trajectory/)

findings.method: Joint ballistic fit across a gap: treat two detected segments separated by a mid-air dropout as one flight if a single (x0, y0, vx, vy, g fixed) model explains both within pixel tolerance, and use the fit to bridge lost frames
findings.how_it_applies: Directly targets the diagnosed failure (only 1 of many Hive entries found because paths are lost mid-air). Balls rising into the Hive Cell from below can be linked through occlusion by requiring one parabola to explain pre-gap and post-gap detections, which also yields the Hive-entry crossing point for the shot classifier. Reject links whose residual exceeds a threshold to avoid merging balls from different robots.
findings.evidence: Constrained parabola / least-squares trajectory fitting as described in the Tracker and fizziq sources above; the general approach of fitting a single ballistic model to tracked positions to read launch parameters (no single paper found that matches this exactly; treat as an engineering extension of the cited parabola-fitting method)

findings.method: Possession-by-nearest-player with a calibrated radius, applied at the launch event (ball-to-agent distance threshold, closest agent wins)
findings.how_it_applies: Adapt the sports rule to launches: at the launch frame (from the existing frame-difference/color launch scanner), assign the shot to the robot whose box is closest to the ball and within a radius. Calibrate the radius empirically in pixels, not from a fixed metric value, since sports papers use per-setup thresholds. This gives a deterministic baseline to compare against the current identity-model attribution, which is failing from track ID swaps.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2509.22522 (JointDiff, multi-agent trajectories): sweeps possession distance 0-3 m and reports about 1.5 m as the threshold where direction change is smallest, assigning possession to the closest player within that radius (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22522; OpenReview version: https://openreview.net/pdf/97d90a1188f72b95ea556fbe60ad2bfafdc81141.pdf). arXiv 2508.09238 (ELASTIC) uses a ~3 m ball-player cutoff to identify the executing player and the closest player at the end frame as receiver (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.09238v1). IJICIC basketball-style video uses a 50 px threshold chosen from 40/50/60 px (http://www.ijicic.org/ijicic-220107.pdf). Note: the 1.5 m and 3 m values were seen in search snippets and only partially verified.

findings.method: Event-anchored, possession-first tracking: track agents and assign possession first, then use agent trajectories to reconstruct the ball, rather than the reverse
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's robot-track identity swaps are the root of the wrong-robot credit. Instead of trusting a persistent robot track ID across the whole match, resolve identity locally at each launch event (the robot that holds/launches the ball at that moment, using roster classifier votes over a short window around the launch). Attribution then depends only on local identity near the launch, which is far less exposed to long-horizon ID swaps.
findings.evidence: Optical tracking in team sports, arXiv 2204.04143 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04143) and 'Take your eyes off the ball: Improving ball-tracking by focusing on team play', Computer Vision and Image Understanding (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1077314213002300) which tracks players and assigns possession first, then reconstructs the ball, for ball-centric sports such as basketball and soccer

findings.method: Sequence model over agent-to-ball possession states (CRF + Viterbi decoding picking one possession edge per time step, flagging an event when the selected edge changes)
findings.how_it_applies: Once several candidate robots are near a ball, a CRF with forbidden transitions can produce a consistent possessor sequence, which prevents attributing one launch to two robots and gives a principled way to handle ambiguous near-robot frames. Needs per-frame robot-ball features; training data would come from the ~20 labeled matches' per-launch reviews.
findings.evidence: PathCRF, arXiv 2602.12080 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12080; HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12080): detects soccer ball-control and pass events from player trajectories only, using a CRF over possession edges with Viterbi decoding. The page reports no quantitative results in the fetched content, so accuracy is unverified.

findings.method: Learned possessor classifier from player-centric features (per-robot likelihood of having launched the ball at each frame)
findings.how_it_applies: Replace the hand-set nearest-robot rule with a small learned scorer over per-robot features (ball-to-box distance, ball velocity direction relative to robot, time since launch, roster identity score) trained on the labeled launches. This generalizes the single-threshold baseline and can be trained cheaply on the existing labels.
findings.evidence: SciTePress 2025 video-based possessor recognition paper, which scores per-player possession likelihood from video and detects passes from possession changes (https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2025/133177/133177.pdf); arXiv 2512.19528 multi-modal soccer model that jointly infers ball state and possessor (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.19528)

findings.method: Commercial sensor-based shot attribution (vendor claim, unverified)
findings.how_it_applies: Shows that shot-to-shooter attribution without wearables is a commercial product category, but the mechanism (arena sensors sampling ball position at a fixed rate and auto-tagging the shooter) is not transferable to a single side-view camera. Not recommended as a method for Robo Scout.
findings.evidence: Noah Basketball products page (https://www.noahbasketball.com/products). Vendor claim only, not independently verified.

recommendation: For Robo Scout, attribute each launch by back-projecting a physics-constrained parabola (fit per flight segment, and across mid-air dropouts with one shared ballistic model) to its launch point and time, then assign the shot to the robot whose box contains or is nearest to that launch point at that frame, using roster identity votes in a short window around the launch rather than the long-run track ID. Calibrate the proximity radius in pixels on the labeled launches and use it as a baseline. Treat the sports possession papers (nearest-player thresholds, possession-first tracking, PathCRF) as supporting methods; none of the sources found describes backtracking a projectile in exactly this setup, and the thresholds (1.5 m, 3 m, 50 px) are setup-specific and only partially verified.

topic: Multi-object tracking for visually similar objects with re-ID (ByteTrack, BoT-SORT, OC-SORT, StrongSORT, Deep OC-SORT) and Ultralytics integration

findings.method: BoT-SORT with ReID (with_reid: True) for robot tracks
findings.how_it_applies: Robot identity swaps happen when two similar robots cross or occlude each other. BoT-SORT fuses IoU and appearance-ReID distance in association, uses camera motion compensation (GMC), and a Kalman state that tracks box width/height. It is the best-documented appearance option in Ultralytics (supported by with_reid). Use it for the 4 robot tracks only. Appearance cues between near-identical robots are weak, so pair it with the team/identity classifier as a per-track vote, not a per-frame label.
findings.evidence: BoT-SORT paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14651 (reports BoT-SORT-ReID 65.0 HOTA, 80.2 IDF1 on MOT17 test, private detector); Ultralytics tracking docs https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track/ (with_reid off by default, supported by BoT-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, TrackTrack)

findings.method: Deep OC-SORT (adaptive appearance gating)
findings.how_it_applies: Deep OC-SORT adds appearance to OC-SORT and adaptively integrates it, so appearance is down-weighted when detector confidence is low (occlusion/blur). This directly targets the failure mode where a robot is partly hidden and its appearance feature is unreliable, which is likely the cause of identity swaps at the moment of crossing. It is listed in Ultralytics as a supported tracker with with_reid. Compare against BoT-SORT-ReID on the held-out match.
findings.evidence: Deep OC-SORT paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11813 (abstract: 63.9 HOTA MOT20, 64.9 HOTA MOT17, 61.3 HOTA DanceTrack; argues heuristic appearance use is not robust to feature degradation); Ultralytics docs https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track/ (tracker_type deepocsort)

findings.method: ByteTrack and OC-SORT (motion-only) for the ball tracks
findings.how_it_applies: Balls are about 10 px and have no useful appearance, so ReID adds nothing. ByteTrack's two-stage association keeps low-confidence detections, which suits small, blurred balls in flight. ByteTrack has no appearance model and no camera-motion compensation, per the Ultralytics docs. OC-SORT's observation-centric re-update is a better fit for objects whose motion changes abruptly. Caveat (my inference, not from the sources): a constant-velocity Kalman filter does not model a ballistic arc. A gravity-aware or quadratic motion model, or segmenting each launch as one trajectory and fitting it, is likely needed to bridge the mid-air gaps that break ball paths.
findings.evidence: Ultralytics docs https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track/ (ByteTrack: no appearance model, no GMC); OC-SORT paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.14360 (observation-centric re-update, same-detection comparison with ByteTrack, 63.2 vs 63.1 HOTA on MOT17 as quoted in the Deep OC-SORT paper)

findings.method: StrongSORT (and StrongSORT++, offline)
findings.how_it_applies: StrongSORT upgrades DeepSORT with a stronger appearance embedding, EMA appearance update, and motion correction. StrongSORT++ adds offline post-processing (link interpolation/association over the whole clip). For this project, the offline post-processing is attractive because the full match video is available in advance, so an offline pass could repair fragmented robot tracks and merge ball segments. Not a fit for live use. I did not fetch the StrongSORT paper; the numbers below come from search snippets only.
findings.evidence: StrongSORT paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.13514; Roboflow comparison https://trackers.roboflow.com/latest/trackers/comparison/ (search snippet: StrongSORT++ 64.4 HOTA on MOT17, offline method)

findings.method: Ultralytics integration: custom tracker YAML and custom ReID weights
findings.how_it_applies: Ultralytics takes tracker=<name>.yaml in model.track(); copy botsort.yaml or deepocsort.yaml, set with_reid: True, and set model to a custom .pt or exported ONNX/torchscript encoder (the default model: auto reuses detector features and falls back to yolo26n-cls.pt). Tuning keys: track_high_thresh, track_low_thresh, new_track_thresh, track_buffer, match_thresh, gmc_method, proximity_thresh (min IoU for a ReID match), appearance_thresh (min appearance similarity). The docs say ReID train/val/predict modes are still under development, so to use a fine-tuned identity backbone for robots you must supply a custom checkpoint or export an embedding model yourself. Older GitHub mirrors of botsort.yaml predate ReID support, so use the installed ultralytics/cfg/trackers files.
findings.evidence: Ultralytics tracking docs https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track/ (config keys, model options, ReID status); Ultralytics default tracker is TrackTrack per the same page, which conflicts with some mirrors that say BoT-SORT, so verify in the installed version

findings.method: Do not rely on tracker ID alone for robot identity: vote per track with the team classifier
findings.how_it_applies: Even the best ReID tracker can swap IDs. Keep a per-track history of the 87%-accurate roster classifier outputs and assign the robot identity by majority vote over a sliding window, and lock identity only when a track is unambiguous (not near another robot). This fixes wrong-robot credit at the scoring step rather than the tracker step.
findings.evidence: Derived from BoT-SORT and Deep OC-SORT paper designs (appearance gated by confidence) cited above; this is a design recommendation, not a sourced result

recommendation: Use BoT-SORT with with_reid: True (or Deep OC-SORT, which adaptively gates appearance under occlusion) for the four robot tracks, with a custom ReID checkpoint if the default auto model cannot separate the robots. Keep ByteTrack (no ReID) or OC-SORT for balls, and fix the mid-air gaps with a ballistic motion model rather than appearance. Attribute shots to robots by majority-voting the identity classifier over each track's history instead of trusting raw tracker IDs. Evaluate on the held-out match by counting ID switches before and after. Note: this was a single-agent research pass; the requested 20-agent research fan-out was not performed here.

topic: FRC/FTC robot tracking, bumper identity, and scoring detection from match video (for Robo Scout)

findings.method: Robot detection on bumpers, not whole robots, with a two-class alliance label (Red/Blue)
findings.how_it_applies: Roboflow's FRC robot-path project labeled bumpers because they reduce overfitting to each year's robot shapes and transfer across seasons. Robo Scout could detect bumpers and classify alliance by color, then use bumper-color/number crops to anchor robot identity instead of relying only on the full-robot team-classifier.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/robot-path-mapping (fetched via redirect from https://blog.roboflow.com/robot-path-mapping/); project code https://github.com/NimbleValley/auto-scout

findings.method: Distance-based greedy tracker run per alliance, with gap handling (skip frames with too few detections)
findings.how_it_applies: The Roboflow project matches detections to the previous frame by sorting pairwise distances and assigning closest pairs first. It is simple, but the author reports no accuracy metrics and skips frames with only one or two detections, which leaves gaps. It is a weak baseline for identity swaps between similar robots, though it may suffice when alliance-level tracks are already separated.
findings.evidence: https://roboflow.com/blog/robot-path-mapping

findings.method: SAHI slicing-aided (tiled) inference for small objects, usable with Ultralytics YOLO
findings.how_it_applies: Yellow Pollen balls are about 10 px in a 1280x720 frame, which is a small-object regime. Running the existing YOLO ball detector on overlapping tiles (and optionally slice-assisted training, as in YOLOv8-SMOT) should raise ball recall before any tracking. SAHI's page lists Ultralytics support, including YOLO26 demos, so it fits the current stack. No accuracy numbers were available on the page.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/obss/sahi (supports ultralytics>=8.3.161 per README); YOLOv8-SMOT code https://github.com/Salvatore-Love/YOLOv8-SMOT (arXiv 2507.12087, slice-assisted training + adaptive association; paper text not extractable, so its numbers are unverified)

findings.method: Occlusion-aware multi-frame ball trajectory network (TOTNet): 3D-conv U-Net over 5 frames, occlusion masking augmentation, visibility-weighted loss
findings.how_it_applies: Hive-cell entries happen when balls rise into the cell and vanish from view, so per-frame detection loses them. TOTNet's occlusion augmentation (masking the ball region in the target frame) and visibility-weighted loss train the model to infer trajectories through occlusion. Reported gains on fully occluded table-tennis frames: RMSE 37.30 to 7.19, accuracy 0.63 to 0.80. The base model runs ~28 FPS and the optical-flow variant ~12 FPS, which suits offline analysis.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.09650v1 (TOTNet, code https://github.com/AugustRushG/TOTNet). Domain is table tennis (TTA dataset), not FRC, so it must be retrained on Robo Scout's footage.

findings.method: TrackNet-family heatmap tracking with trajectory rectification (TrackNetV3 repair masks); TrackNetV4 motion attention
findings.how_it_applies: TrackNet is a multi-frame heatmap network built for tiny fast sports objects (original paper reports F1 98.5% on tennis). TrackNetV3 adds trajectory rectification to repair errors, which targets the missed-detection problem. TrackNetV4 adds frame-differencing motion attention and claims gains on occlusion, but its abstract gives no numbers. A master's thesis on football found TrackNet fails when the ball is still or frequently occluded, which matters for balls that sit in the cell.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.03698 (TrackNet, arXiv 1907.03698); https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.14543 (TrackNetV4, no code link found); thesis via https://odr.chalmers.se/server/api/core/bitstreams/a09ccd10-bc5a-4afe-aa6e-3fe4498e3897/content

findings.method: Kalman trackers with observation-centric re-update (OC-SORT) for nonlinear motion and occlusion gaps
findings.how_it_applies: OC-SORT corrects Kalman error accumulated during occlusion by using detector observations to build a virtual trajectory across the gap. A 2025 study on fast tiny objects found DeepOCSORT had ADE 31.15 px versus ByteTrack's 114.3 px (ByteTrack fastest). For Robo Scout, this suggests replacing or augmenting ByteTrack-style IoU association for balls with an OC-SORT-style or DeepOCSORT-style tracker, and gap-filling with the same virtual-trajectory idea.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14360 (OC-SORT, CVPR 2023, code https://github.com/noahcao/OC_SORT); https://arxiv.org/html/2509.18451v1 (Kalman trackers on fast tiny objects, ADE numbers from search snippet)

findings.method: Appearance (ReID) association for identity, since IoU-only trackers swap IDs among similar objects
findings.how_it_applies: Sources say ByteTrack relies only on IoU matching and gets more ID switches when objects overlap or are occluded. BoT-SORT adds a ReID appearance term plus Gaussian-based matching. For Robo Scout's identity swaps between similar robots, an appearance term (bumper color or team-number crop embedding) inside the association step should reduce swaps. Caveat: appearance is often unreliable on very small targets, so use it only for robot-scale boxes, not balls.
findings.evidence: BoT-SORT via search summary (arXiv/benchmark snippet, no direct figure); ByteTrack IoU weakness per https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.17521 (CORT, class-oriented tracking) snippet; Basketball-SORT for occlusion between same-looking players https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.19655 (PDF not extractable; cited by title only, unverified)

findings.method: Gap-filling in tracks: linear or GSI interpolation, or learned masked-imputation of missing trajectory points
findings.how_it_applies: The SoccerNet 2023 MOT4MOT report linearly interpolates missing detections, and another team uses GSI interpolation plus a learned link model. A learned imputation approach masks ground-truth ball points and trains a model to fill them. For Robo Scout, these could recover single-ball trajectories through the Hive Cell instead of the current 1 of many entries detected.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.16651 (SoccerNet 2023 MOT4MOT, 3rd place); ball imputation https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.08206 (Set Transformer + Bi-LSTM ball trajectory inference)

findings.method: Robot-path mapping pipelines and FRC datasets exist, but no open-source FRC shot/scoring counter was found
findings.how_it_applies: Searches found no FRC project that counts game pieces or hive scores from video, and no paper on FRC game-piece scouting. Roboflow Universe has FRC robot-detection and game-piece datasets (e.g., https://universe.roboflow.com/ctrlz-4096/frc-game-piece, description unverified). Team 1706's vision2015 repo is robot-side, not match-video. The Statbotics/TBA search found no video-based piece counting. The FTC docs note OpenCV color blob detection as a simpler alternative for colored pieces, which matches Robo Scout's color-blob launch scanner.
findings.evidence: https://blog.roboflow.com/robot-path-mapping/ ; https://universe.roboflow.com/frc-robot-tracking/frc-robot-detection-reefscape ; https://github.com/rr1706/vision2015 ; https://ftc-docs.firstinspires.org/en/latest/programming_resources/vision/vision_overview/vision-overview.html

recommendation: Rank fixes by the stated problems. (1) Ball recall: run the existing YOLO ball detector with SAHI-style tiled inference (or slice-assisted training per YOLOv8-SMOT) so the ~10 px Pollen balls are detected. (2) Hive entries: replace per-frame ball-in-cell detection with a TOTNet-style occlusion-aware multi-frame model trained on Robo Scout's labeled matches (occlusion masking augmentation + visibility-weighted loss), and fill gaps with GSI or linear interpolation on tracks. (3) Identity: move robot tracking from IoU-only association to an OC-SORT or BoT-SORT-style tracker with a bumper-color or team-number appearance term, and anchor the robot tracks to bumpers rather than full robots. (4) Keep the color-blob launch scanner as the cheap baseline. Caveat: no source tested these on FRC footage; TOTNet and TrackNet numbers come from table tennis and tennis.

topic: Team number / jersey number OCR for robot identity (PARSeq, SoccerNet jersey pipelines)

findings.method: PARSeq scene-text recognizer applied to jersey numbers, frame-level reads then tracklet-level aggregation
findings.how_it_applies: Read the printed team number on each robot's bumper/body crop per frame with PARSeq (or a fine-tuned copy), then aggregate reads over a robot track. This gives a direct identity signal that does not depend on the per-team YOLO classifier (87% roster accuracy). Use the aggregated number as an identity anchor and re-anchor tracks whenever a confident read appears, which addresses track-ID swaps between similar robots.
findings.evidence: Koshkina & Elder 2024, 'A General Framework for Jersey Number Recognition in Sports Video', https://arxiv.org/html/2405.13896v1 (PARSeq-based detection, localization, frame-level recognition; reported 91.4% on hockey images and 87.4% on soccer tracklets, per search snippet; full paper not opened). PARSeq: Bautista & Atienza, ECCV 2022, arXiv 2207.06966, reference code https://github.com/baudm/parseq (pretrained parseq-tiny/parseq variants available, PyTorch Hub).

findings.method: Legible-frame classifier before aggregation (keep only frames where the number is readable, then vote or average)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's frames are small (team numbers likely tens of pixels at 1280x720). Train or use a simple legibility/confidence gate on each crop and only vote with frames above threshold. The 2024 paper found simpler aggregation competitive once legible frames are selected, so a confidence-weighted majority vote over a track is a cheap first version.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2405.13896 (classifier flags legible frames, then aggregates; simpler aggregation methods competitive, per search snippet). Balaji et al. 2023 keyframe identification, arXiv 2309.06285, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.06285 (keyframe module gave reported 37.8% and 37.7% accuracy gains on two domain-gap test sets, per snippet).

findings.method: Torso/number-region localization with keypoints or a detector before OCR, plus restoration and confidence-weighted ensemble
findings.how_it_applies: Crop the team-number region first (a small YOLO detector trained on a few hundred labeled crops, or a fixed offset from the robot box), optionally upscale or restore, then run OCR. A 2025-era pipeline reportedly restored inputs and ensembled PARSeq with vision-language models using confidence weighting, improving tracklet accuracy over baseline. Relevant because a team-number read is more reliable than the roster classifier alone.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet 2025 Challenges Results, arXiv 2508.19182, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.19182 (torso extraction then PARSeq OCR). UBC Okanagan ensemble paper described in search results only; source URL not captured, so treat as unverified.

findings.method: SoccerNet jersey number benchmark and sn-jersey tooling as labeled-data and evaluation reference
findings.how_it_applies: SoccerNet 2023 defines tracklet-level jersey number recognition (2853 training/test tracklets, hidden challenge set; top reported 92.85%). The sn-jersey repo can supply the evaluation protocol and training code for a tracklet-level metric. Robo Scout can adopt the tracklet-level accuracy metric to measure identity fixes per robot.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet 2023 Challenges Results, arXiv 2309.06006, https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06006; sn-jersey repo https://github.com/SoccerNet/sn-jersey (per search snippets).

findings.method: Single-stage digit-compositional classifier with uncertainty (alternative to PARSeq)
findings.how_it_applies: If a fixed set of team numbers exists (the roster), a closed-set classifier over the roster with Dirichlet uncertainty can run cheaper than a full sequence recognizer and abstain when unsure, which fits Robo Scout's closed roster. Reported 85.62% tracklet accuracy on the SoccerNet challenge benchmark.
findings.evidence: CVPR 2025 sports workshop single-stage uncertainty-aware method, https://cvpr.thecvf.com/virtual/2025/35507 (only the search snippet was seen; the exact paper title was not captured).

recommendation: Add a per-frame PARSeq read of the team number on each robot crop, gate on legibility or confidence, and aggregate by confident-vote per track; use a confident read to re-anchor the robot's identity whenever it appears. Ground truth for evaluation: SoccerNet-style tracklet-level accuracy on your ~20 labeled videos. Caveat: all numbers here come from search snippets and abstracts; the full papers were not read, and the FTC team-number visibility on robots in this broadcast view has not been checked.

topic: Temporal action spotting for Robo Scout: SoccerNet action spotting, E2E-Spot, T-DEED, feasibility with ~20 labeled matches

findings.method: E2E-Spot: end-to-end trained frame encoder plus temporal head for precise event timestamps
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's shot-release and Hive-entry events are single-timestamp events in long untrimmed video, the exact task E2E-Spot targets. Its key claim is that training the frame feature extractor end-to-end with the spotting head beats two-stage pipelines (frozen features, then a separate classifier), which is close to the current frame-difference plus per-frame detector plus logistic-classifier stack. The paper says it trains quickly on a single GPU, relevant for Apple Silicon. The jhong93/spot README says it expects pre-extracted frames at about 224 px high, laid out as video/frame.jpg, and gives the training command train_e2e.py <dataset> <frame_dir> -s <save_dir> -m <arch>. It lists datasets tennis, fs_comp, fs_perf, finediving, finegym, soccernetv2 and soccernet_ball, and does not mention MPS or CPU support, so porting is a risk.
findings.evidence: Hong et al., Spotting Temporally Precise, Fine-Grained Events in Video, ECCV 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10213 (abstract: compact end-to-end model, trains quickly on a single GPU, outperforms recent baselines). Code: https://github.com/jhong93/spot (README fetched). Second-place 2022 SoccerNet challenge result taken from search snippet, not verified in the paper body.

findings.method: T-DEED: temporal-discriminability encoder-decoder with full-resolution multi-scale output for precise spotting
findings.how_it_applies: T-DEED targets three problems that match Robo Scout's failure modes: adjacent frames that look nearly identical (the ball is about 10 px and moves little per frame), the need for output at full temporal resolution to hit tight timing tolerances, and events with different dynamics at several time scales. Its ablation (FS-Comp, delta=1 mAP) shows SGP-Mixer with skip connections at 77.96 vs 74.29 with no skips, and GSF in the back half of the backbone is best. Clip length 100 frames was best (81.25) vs 25 frames (71.02). Soft-NMS over 50%-overlapping clips beat plain NMS (85.15 vs 81.27). Tuned recipe: AdamW, base LR 8e-4, 3 warmup epochs, cosine decay, 50 epochs, batch 8 clips, 5000 clips per epoch, weighted cross-entropy (w=5) plus MSE for displacement, mixup alpha=0.2. Directly relevant to the lost-mid-air and missed-entry problems: overlapping clips with a temporal encoder-decoder can recover events whose trajectory breaks in one frame window. T-DEED won 1st place in the 2024 SoccerNet Ball Action Spotting challenge per search snippet from the revised paper, a sports setting with a small ball. That claim was not verified in the paper body.
findings.evidence: Xarles et al., T-DEED, arXiv:2404.05392 (v2 HTML read: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.05392v2 ; abstract https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05392). Code: https://github.com/arturxe2/T-DEED. Challenge result: SoccerNet 2024 Challenges Results https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.10587 (search snippet only).

findings.method: Feasibility with ~20 labeled matches: spotting heads on frozen or lightly tuned pretrained backbones with sparse labels
findings.how_it_applies: The papers' training sets are small and label density is sparse. FigureSkating has 11 videos, 371 performances, and annotations on about 0.23% of frames. FineDiving has 3,000 clips with about 2.2% of frames annotated. So a spotting head trained on roughly 20 matches' worth of per-launch labels is in a plausible regime, but the paper does not state a minimum training-set size, so this is inference. Ways to reduce risk: start from T-DEED or E2E-Spot pretrained weights where available, augment with the public SoccerNet Ball data, and use the delta=1 and delta=2 frame tolerance metrics for evaluation so timing gains are measurable. A held-out match split is needed because the reported numbers are on public benchmarks. The 20-match dataset is too small to train the full backbone from scratch, which is consistent with the papers' use of pretrained RegNetY features.
findings.evidence: FigureSkating and FineDiving dataset sizes and annotation density from T-DEED v2 HTML (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.05392v2). Metrics delta=1 and delta=2 from same source.

findings.method: SoccerNet action spotting as the benchmark family; ball action spotting challenge as a reference point
findings.how_it_applies: SoccerNet defines action spotting as localizing an action with one timestamp in untrimmed video, and has a dedicated ball action spotting track that is closest to small-object events. Using SoccerNet-Ball as an external pretraining or validation source for the spotting head is the most realistic way to get more labeled timing data beyond 20 matches. OSL-ActionSpotting is a unified library that re-implements E2E-Spot and other spotting methods, and can serve as a reference to check the port against.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet 2024 challenges results https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.10587 ; review https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.01304 (PDF not readable by the fetch tool, not used for specific claims) ; OSL-ActionSpotting https://arxiv.org/html/2407.01265v1 (search snippet only).

recommendation: Replace the current per-frame-detector-plus-logistic-classifier shot and entry logic with a T-DEED or E2E-Spot style spotting head: per-frame features from a pretrained backbone, overlapping 100-frame clips with the SGP-style encoder-decoder kept at full temporal resolution, and Soft-NMS over the overlapping windows. Train it on the ~20 labeled matches plus SoccerNet-Ball, evaluate with delta=1 and delta=2 frame tolerances on held-out matches, and port the CUDA-oriented jhong93/spot or arturxe2/T-DEED code to MPS, checking the port against OSL-ActionSpotting.

topic: Motion-based small object detection (frame differencing, MOG2/KNN, optical flow, motion+color+CNN verifier) for fast small balls in Robo Scout

findings.method: TrackNet: heatmap CNN for tiny fast balls, frame-stacked input (640x360), Gaussian-target heatmap, threshold 128; trajectory-aware via consecutive frames
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's YOLO ball detector misses fast/blurred balls. A frame-stacked heatmap network learns ball trajectory cues and can recover the ball when single-frame detection fails. Reports tennis F1 84.3% (10-fold CV), 98.5% on one final. Could replace or verify YOLO26 ball detections using 3 consecutive frames.
findings.evidence: Huang et al., TrackNet, arXiv 1907.03698, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.03698 (fetched abstract page)

findings.method: TrackNetV4 motion-aware fusion: absolute frame-difference maps |I_t - I_{t-1}| modulated by a learnable motion prompt layer, fused with visual features via motion attention; plug-and-play on TrackNetV2/V3
findings.how_it_applies: Direct template for adding a motion channel to Robo Scout's ball detector: compute frame differences in the launch/cell region, feed them as an extra attention input so balls that differ from the static background are emphasized. Paper gives no numeric gains in the abstract, so validate on the 20 labeled videos.
findings.evidence: TrackNetV4, arXiv 2409.14543, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14543 (fetched); abstract-level results only

findings.method: TrackNetV5 Motion Direction Decoupling: frame differencing that keeps the sign/direction (plain absolute difference discards sign), claimed to approximate optical-flow directional clarity at frame-differencing cost
findings.how_it_applies: Balls rising into the Hive Cell from below have a consistent upward direction; signed motion cues would separate rising launches from static robots and background clutter. Only seen in search snippets of arXiv 2512.02789 (unverified in full).
findings.evidence: arXiv 2512.02789 (v2/v3), https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02789 (search snippet only, not fully read)

findings.method: FMO (Fast Moving Object) streak detection and trajectory fitting: model a fast object as a semi-transparent streak over exposure; detector, redetector, tracker pipeline; 16-video FMO dataset; existing trackers judged inadequate
findings.how_it_applies: Balls moving more than their own size per frame (Pollen ~10 px at launch speed, 60 fps) appear as streaks. Treating a launch as a streak-trajectory fit can recover shots that a per-frame detector breaks up mid-air, which matches the 'ball paths lost mid-air' failure. Reconstructing the path as one object across gaps is the key idea for counting shots.
findings.evidence: Rozumnyi et al., The World of Fast Moving Objects, CVPR 2017, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_cvpr_2017/html/Rozumnyi_The_World_of_CVPR_2017_paper.html and arXiv 1611.07889

findings.method: FMODetect: learned detection of fast moving objects via a matting-and-fitting network (estimates blurred appearance without background and fits trajectory) trained on synthetic data, plus energy-minimization deblurring; claims higher recall/precision than prior methods, real-time
findings.how_it_applies: Synthetic-data training of a streak/trajectory detector could be a way to get more labeled motion examples than the ~20 labeled videos. Speed and metric claims are vague on the page, so treat as directional.
findings.evidence: Rozumnyi et al., FMODetect, ICCV 2021, arXiv 2012.08216, https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08216 (fetched abstract page)

findings.method: MOG2 (Zivkovic 2004 adaptive GMM) background subtraction, OpenCV cv::createBackgroundSubtractorMOG2(history, varThreshold, detectShadows); a forum report says plain absdiff against a background beat MOG/MOG2 for a small drone
findings.how_it_applies: Use as a cheap candidate generator in a fixed camera scene (the broadcast camera is fixed), with shadows disabled and a short history so a fast ball stays foreground; prefer a frame-difference or absdiff baseline first since MOG2 absorbs slow-moving or stationary balls into background. Benchmark against absdiff on the 20 videos.
findings.evidence: Zivkovic, Improved adaptive GMM for background subtraction, ICPR 2004, https://dare.uva.nl/id/5655e0ce-f18f-471f-af8a-153f45565e51; OpenCV MOG2 docs https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/d7/d7b/classcv_1_1BackgroundSubtractorMOG2.html; OpenCV forum https://answers.opencv.org/question/181336/improve-opencv-background-subtraction/

findings.method: RAFT dense optical flow (Teed and Deng, ECCV 2020; all-pairs correlation with iterative refinement; official code github.com/princeton-vl/RAFT) as a motion mask/feature source
findings.how_it_applies: Accurate but heavy for a 60 fps full-frame pipeline on Apple Silicon MPS; more practical to compute flow only in a cropped region of interest around the Hive Cell and launch zones, or use Farneback (OpenCV, cheaper) for candidate motion. Flow magnitude plus direction gives a launch-direction feature for the shot classifier.
findings.evidence: Teed and Deng, RAFT, ECCV 2020, arXiv 2003.12039, https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12039

findings.method: Two-stage motion-candidate then CNN verifier: frame differences or AND-combined differences, filter connected components by size/shape/aspect ratio, then a CNN classifies each candidate; classical FMO-style pipelines and TrackNet-family work use this pattern
findings.how_it_applies: Most direct fix for missed shots: generate motion blobs (absdiff/MOG2 mask) and color-filter them for Pollen/Nectar hues, keep components of ball size (~10 px), then verify with the existing YOLO26 ball classifier or the trajectory-feature logistic model. Recovers balls YOLO misses while limiting false positives from robots and the score overlay.
findings.evidence: TrackNet arXiv 1907.03698 (AND-combined differences plus shape/size filter); arXiv 2003.03856 baseball tracking (thresholded difference with minimum connected-component area), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.03856; PMC8124271 YOLOv3 small fast ball detection, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8124271

recommendation: Build a motion-candidate stage before the YOLO ball detector: MOG2 (shadows off, short history) or absdiff on a fixed-camera ROI, intersected with a color mask for Pollen/Nectar and filtered to ~10 px blobs. Feed candidates and a 3-frame signed frame-difference stack into a TrackNet-style verifier (or the existing YOLO26 classifier) and link detections into per-launch streaks for trajectory fitting, so a launch is one object across gaps. Validate on the 20 labeled videos; treat TrackNetV4/V5 gains and FMODetect speed claims as unverified until checked against full papers.

topic: Training and inference for very small objects (~10 px balls) with Ultralytics YOLO11/YOLO26: SAHI, tiling, imgsz, P2 head, anchor-free settings

findings.method: Ultralytics built-in tile argument (replaces the SAHI integration for training, validation and prediction)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout balls are ~10 px in a 1280x720 frame. Running at imgsz=640 downsamples by 2x, leaving ~5 px objects. tile=True processes overlapping windows at native resolution before resizing, so balls keep detail. Use model.train(..., tile=True, imgsz=640) to create training tiles with clipped labels (negative windows kept), and predict with tile=True to get one Results per original frame. Caveat: tiling drops global context and adds forward passes, so verify on the labeled match videos (especially the Hive cell and robot-level behavior, which need context).
findings.evidence: https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/high-resolution-tiling (tile argument; training example model.train(data='aerial.yaml', tile=True, imgsz=640); caveats on forward passes and lost global context)

findings.method: SAHI sliced inference with AutoDetectionModel (ultralytics model_type), inference-only, no retraining
findings.how_it_applies: Slices a 1280x720 frame into overlapping tiles, runs YOLO per tile, merges boxes. This is a cheap way to test whether the existing YOLO26 ball detector recovers missed small balls without retraining. Ultralytics docs use 256 px or 512 px slices with 0.2 overlap in examples. The Ultralytics SAHI guide itself is now marked deprecated in favor of tile, so use SAHI as an external baseline/comparison rather than the primary path. The sahi tool supports YOLO26 and sahi predict --model_type ultralytics.
findings.evidence: https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/sahi-tiled-inference (deprecation banner; slice 256/overlap 0.2 examples; AutoDetectionModel usage); https://obss.github.io/sahi/guides/models/ and https://github.com/obss/SAHI (SAHI compatible-model list incl. Ultralytics YOLOv8/YOLO11/YOLO26)

findings.method: Original SAHI paper: inference-time slicing and slicing-aware fine-tuning
findings.how_it_applies: Reports AP gains on VisDrone and xView: inference-only slicing +6.8% (FCOS), +5.1% (VFNet), +5.3% (TOOD); adding slicing-aware fine-tuning raised the cumulative gain to 12.7%, 13.4%, 14.5%. Supports the plan to fine-tune on sliced crops of the labeled videos, not just slice at inference. Gains are for aerial datasets, so they are an expectation, not a guarantee for 10 px balls.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06934 (Akyon, Altinuc, Temizel, ICIP 2022; abstract numbers)

findings.method: Evaluation of YOLOv5/YOLOX with sliced inference on VisDrone
findings.how_it_applies: Sliced inference increased AP50 in all experiments, larger gain for YOLOv5 than YOLOX; sliced fine-tuning added further gains. Top result YOLOv5-L AP50 48.8 on VisDrone2019Det test-dev. Paper does not report full-image baselines or latency, so use it only as directional evidence.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04799

findings.method: YOLO26 P2 detection head (yolo26-p2.yaml)
findings.how_it_applies: Adds a stride-4 P2 head for small objects. Important: no pretrained yolo26*-p2.pt weights are released. Build from the YAML and transfer from yolo26n.pt (Ultralytics guide: Train a YOLO26 P2 Model from Pretrained Weights). Stride-4 features help 10 px objects, but cost compute and memory at 1280-class input, so pair it with tile or a higher imgsz and check MPS speed. A third-party 2026 paper (SDD-YOLO) applies P2 with YOLO26-style components to sub-16 px UAV targets, which is directly analogous.
findings.evidence: https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/ (yolo26-p2.yaml; 'No scale-specific yolo26*-p2.pt ... weights are released'); https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25218v1 (SDD-YOLO, P2 at 4x downsampling for sub-16 px)

findings.method: YOLO26 small-object training features: STAL and ProgLoss
findings.how_it_applies: Docs describe STAL (Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment) to improve positive label coverage for small objects and Progressive Loss (ProgLoss) shifting emphasis toward the inference head. These are built in, so no custom code is needed. Verify the effect with per-class recall on ball crops rather than assuming it.
findings.evidence: https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/

findings.method: imgsz choice
findings.how_it_applies: Ultralytics YOLO26 docs give no small-object imgsz recommendation and use 640 as the default example. For ~10 px balls, 640 full-frame loses too much detail (about 5 px). Test imgsz 960 or 1280 at full-frame, or tile, rather than relying on 640. Cost scales roughly with pixel count, so 1280 is about 4x the 640 compute.
findings.evidence: https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/yolo26/ (imgsz benchmarks listed; no small-object guidance); arithmetic from 1280x720 source resolution

recommendation: For Robo Scout, the highest-value and lowest-cost change is to stop running the ball detector at imgsz=640 on the full 1280x720 frame, which shrinks 10 px balls to about 5 px. First, benchmark the existing YOLO26 ball detector with inference-only tiling (Ultralytics predict with tile=True at imgsz 640, or SAHI with ~256-512 px slices and 0.2 overlap) against the current baseline on a few labeled matches, measuring per-ball recall. Second, retrain the ball detector with tile=True on the labeled videos (keep negative windows) so it learns from native-resolution crops, and test whether the yolo26-p2.yaml P2 head (built from YAML, initialized from yolo26n.pt, since no P2 weights exist) adds recall at acceptable MPS speed. Keep the robot/identity models at full frame, because tiling drops global context. Expected gains are directional: the cited SAHI results are +5 to +7% AP inference-only on aerial data, and +12 to +15% with slicing-aware fine-tuning, not measured on balls. Measure against the full-frame baseline on held-out matches before committing.

topic: Kalman filter and physics-based (parabolic) trajectory tracking for small balls through occlusion and missed detections; gating, track birth/death, fragment linking

findings.method: Constant-velocity Kalman filter with coasting through missed detections (predict-only, no correction), with process noise inflated as the occlusion lengthens
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout loses ball paths mid-air. Keep each ball track alive by predicting forward with no update during misses, and cap the coast length so the prediction horizon cannot diverge. Tune Q/R per scenario, since the paper reports they are not given numerically and must be tuned.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.18451v1 (analysis of KF trackers for fast tiny objects; notes Q/R must be tuned per scenario). Occlusion skip-update and adaptive Q inflation described in search summaries of arXiv 2603.09783 (LiDAR UAV tracker, reinitializes after a fixed number of missed steps to bound the prediction horizon).

findings.method: Warning on linear KF for balls: constant-velocity KF fails on fast, non-linear balls
findings.how_it_applies: The same paper reports that linear constant-velocity KF trackers (DeepOCSORT, OCSORT, StrongSORT, BoTSORT, ByteTrack) give average displacement errors of roughly 20 to 215 px on a fast racquetball task, and failure modes include direction changes, bounces and motion blur. A plain KF will not fix Robo Scout alone. Ballistic segments need a physics model, not a linear one.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.18451v1 (ADE/AMD table; ByteTrack 39 to 215 px, DeepOCSORT 20 to 50 px across four scenarios). Note the paper also has a unit inconsistency between its abstract and its 1 px = 0.026 cm calibration, so use the table values only as relative comparisons.

findings.method: Piecewise parabolic (gravity-constrained) trajectory model fit with RANSAC over short windows, with segmentation at discontinuities
findings.how_it_applies: Fit y(t) and x(t) as quadratic or linear in time per segment, optionally fixing vertical acceleration to gravity in image units (a per-camera scale or homography is needed, since the side view is not metric). RANSAC over small subsets of ball detections rejects false detections such as the yellow Pollen confusion. Break segments at launch, at the cell contact, and at settling. This gives a robust per-launch trajectory, and the parabola can bridge gaps that a Kalman filter cannot.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.03633 (Intra-frame Object Tracking by Deblatting: RANSAC finds linear and quadratic segments, joined into a piecewise trajectory, quadratic for gravity and breaks for bounces). US Patent 11138744 and US 12478848 (fix gravity at -9.8 m/s^2 to reduce unknowns; fit only in-air heights). US 12154284 (sample small subsets of 2D detections, fit a curve, keep the one with most inliers, robust to detector errors).

findings.method: Mahalanobis-distance gating on the Kalman predicted position, instead of IoU gating, before assignment
findings.how_it_applies: IoU between boxes of about 10 px is very brittle, and SORT's IoU gate is designed for larger boxes. Gate each candidate detection with squared Mahalanobis distance from the predicted position using the innovation covariance, against a chi-square threshold. This is the usual gate in trackers, and it suits small fast objects better than IoU. Robo Scout's per-robot identity problem could also use gated candidates, with the identity model used only inside the gate.
findings.evidence: Mahalanobis gating summarized in search results for arXiv 2603.09783 (accept a candidate only if its squared Mahalanobis distance from the predicted measurement falls below a threshold). SORT's IoU+Hungarian baseline: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.00763 and https://github.com/abewley/sort (notes it does not handle occlusion or re-entering objects). The SORT abstract page itself was fetched but did not give the gate details.

findings.method: Two-stage association that keeps low-confidence detections (ByteTrack) to recover occluded or faint balls
findings.how_it_applies: Match high-score detections to tracks first, then match the leftover tracks against low-score detections, which are often the occluded or motion-blurred ball. Unmatched low-score boxes are discarded. This directly targets ball path loss mid-air and reduces missed shots.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06864 (ByteTrack: uses low-score detections, similarity to tracklets recovers occluded objects, filters background. MOT17 test: MOTA 80.3, IDF1 77.3, HOTA 63.1, 30 FPS on V100). The abstract says the association step improved IDF1 by 1 to 10 points when added to nine other trackers.

findings.method: Track birth confirmation and death rules: confirm a track after M consecutive hits, delete after N consecutive misses (SORT probation and max_age)
findings.how_it_applies: Stops false yellow-ball births from the frame-difference scanner from becoming shots, and ends a ball track when it settles inside or below the Cell. Use min_hits around 3 and a max-age tuned to the expected flight time in frames at 60 fps (flights are short, so a few tens of frames of coasting is plausible; this value is a guess to tune, not a sourced number).
findings.evidence: Confirmation after 3 consecutive matched detections (KF_MIN_HITS = 3): summary of a search result on Kalman tracking of tiny objects (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.18451v1 and linked tracking papers). SORT probation and max_age termination: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.00763 (the abstract page did not give the numbers).

findings.method: Physics-guided kinematic tracking with an outlier and missed-detection module for fast small objects
findings.how_it_applies: A 2025 approach integrates kinematic motion equations and an outlier detection and correction module, and reports up to 70% lower average displacement error than KF trackers on a racquetball dataset. The model equations were not visible in the abstract, so the design should be checked in the full paper before copying it. It is the closest published analogue to Robo Scout's ballistic-ball problem.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20126 (Physics-Guided Fusion for Robust 3D Tracking of Fast Moving Small Objects; abstract only, full text not read).

findings.method: Learned physics priors for ball trajectory reconstruction from 2D tracks
findings.how_it_applies: A learned model trained on simulated physics predicts a height per 2D point so the reconstruction matches the input track. It avoids hand-tuned segmentation, but it needs simulated training data and is a larger change than the other methods.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.05763v1 (Where Is The Ball: 3D Ball Trajectory Estimation From 2D Monocular Tracking).

recommendation: Replace the per-frame frame-to-frame linker with a ballistic track model. For each candidate ball track, use a Kalman or RANSAC-fit parabola with a gated (Mahalanobis, not IoU) assignment, two-stage association that keeps low-confidence detections (ByteTrack), coasting through misses with a bounded horizon, and birth/death by M-of-N hits and max-age. Link fragments by fitting one parabola across a gap between one track's end and another's start, and accept the link only if the fitted launch and apex are physically consistent. Count a Hive Cell entry from the fitted trajectory intersecting the cell region, not from a per-frame box. Verify the gravity fit and gate thresholds on the ~20 labeled videos, since none of the sources reports numbers for this domain.

topic: Video clip classification for made/miss or shot/no-shot: X3D, VideoMAE, SlowFast, small 3D CNNs on short crops; data needs and Apple Silicon feasibility

findings.method: X3D (Expanding Architectures for Efficient Video Recognition) as the default small 3D CNN for short-crop clip classification
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's shot clips are short crops around a launch or Hive Cell region, so an efficient 3D CNN fits. X3D-XS/S are the cheapest variants (PyTorchVideo table lists X3D-XS ~0.91 GFLOPs/view, X3D-S ~2.96 GFLOPs/view, both ~3.8M params, 3 spatial x 10 temporal views). A clip classifier could be fine-tuned from Kinetics-400 weights on the ~20 labeled matches with per-launch reviews, using a 2-class head (made/miss) or 2-class shot/no-shot head. Original paper reports X3D-M is comparable to SlowFast 4x16 R50 on AVA at about 5.8x fewer FLOPs, so the efficiency argument is primary-sourced.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.04730 (X3D paper); https://pytorchvideo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/model_zoo.html (PyTorchVideo model zoo table); https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09887 (PyTorchVideo library paper, X3D-L 77.4 top-1 Kinetics-400, 26.6x3x10 GFLOPs, 6.2M params); https://pytorch.org/hub/facebookresearch_pytorchvideo_x3d/ (torch hub loading)

findings.method: SlowFast two-pathway 3D CNN as a heavier alternative when temporal context matters (long trajectories, rising-into-cell motion)
findings.how_it_applies: SlowFast pairs a slow pathway (low frame rate, spatial semantics) with a fast pathway (high frame rate, motion). For a 60 fps broadcast, the fast path can capture rapid ball motion near launch. It costs more than X3D, so it is a second-tier option if X3D underfits on the trajectory-heavy shot class. Reported Kinetics-400 result: 79.8 top-1 for SlowFast 16x8 R101+NL; Charades 42.1 mAP vs 39.0 for Slow-only baseline (values from the paper; Kinetics-600 81.8 and AVA 28.3 were from secondary text and should be verified in the full paper).
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.03982 (SlowFast Networks for Video Recognition, Feichtenhofer et al., ICCV 2019); https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/html/Feichtenhofer_SlowFast_Networks_for_Video_Recognition_ICCV_2019_paper.html; https://github.com/facebookresearch/SlowFast/blob/master/MODEL_ZOO.md

findings.method: VideoMAE self-supervised video transformer, fine-tuned on a small labeled set
findings.how_it_applies: VideoMAE uses masked autoencoding with tube masking at 90-95% ratio and is explicitly positioned for small datasets (paper reports strong results on datasets of around 3k-4k videos without extra data). Relevant to Robo Scout because only ~20 labeled matches exist. Caveat: ViT-B/L backbones are heavier than X3D-S; the paper's own Kinetics-400 numbers are 83.9 (v1) and 87.4 (v3) for the vanilla ViT, so cite the version used. Plausible plan: start from a public VideoMAE checkpoint and fine-tune only the head or last blocks on clip crops; expect higher cost on MPS than X3D-S.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.12602 (VideoMAE, Tong et al., NeurIPS 2022); https://nips.cc/virtual/2022/poster/54362; code https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VideoMAE

findings.method: Apple Silicon (MPS) feasibility check for Conv3d before committing to any 3D CNN
findings.how_it_applies: Conv3d on MPS has historically failed (RuntimeError 'Conv3D is not supported on MPS' and NotImplementedError aten::slow_conv3d_forward reports); PyTorch MPS op-coverage issue #77764 lists nn.Conv3D as requested. Newer reports suggest a Conv3D smoke test passes on recent PyTorch (a forum post cites PyTorch 2.13 MPS convolution), but this is unverified. PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 can route unsupported ops to CPU at a speed cost, and transposed Conv3d was reported separately as failing. Action: run a one-line Conv3d and ConvTranspose3d test on the installed torch version before designing around X3D/SlowFast on MPS. If it fails, a 2D-per-frame encoder with a small temporal head (frame-stack or 2D CNN + temporal pooling) avoids Conv3d entirely.
findings.evidence: https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/will-the-conv3d-operation-be-supported-on-mps-through-pytorch/198233; https://huggingface.co/cerspense/zeroscope_v2_XL/discussions/7; https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/77764 (MPS op coverage tracker, referenced in forum post); https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/100674 (MaxPool3D on MPS); https://plato.cgl.ucsf.edu/trac/ChimeraX/ticket/17832 (fallback workaround report)

findings.method: Reproducibility caution when choosing among X3D, SlowFast, VideoMAE: compare only matched protocols
findings.how_it_applies: Published accuracy numbers differ across sources for the same model (e.g., X3D-L 77.4 in PyTorchVideo paper vs 76.9 in PySlowFast zoo with different GFLOPs). Robo Scout should choose by its own held-out per-launch evaluation, not by Kinetics leaderboard numbers. A reproducibility study attributes much of the apparent progress to unfair evaluation protocols.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09887; https://github.com/facebookresearch/SlowFast/blob/master/MODEL_ZOO.md; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.11757 (A Comprehensive Study of Deep Video Action Recognition / reproducibility discussion referenced by search)

recommendation: Run a Conv3d/ConvTranspose3d smoke test on MPS first. If it passes, fine-tune X3D-S (Kinetics-400 weights, PyTorchVideo) as a binary made/miss classifier on short crops around each launch and Hive Cell region, using the ~20 labeled matches with leave-one-match-out validation; escalate to SlowFast only if X3D underfits trajectory cases, and consider VideoMAE only if fine-tuning a transformer is affordable on MPS. If Conv3d fails on MPS, use a 2D per-frame encoder with temporal pooling instead.

topic: Scoreboard/score-overlay OCR as weak supervision or consistency check for event counts in sports video (for Robo Scout Hive Cell / shot counting)

findings.method: Score-overlay change detection as a consistency oracle: locate the score box per frame, read it, and treat each monotonic increment of the score as a ground-truth event time. Bounds the count of scoring events per alliance and gives the event timestamps that the shot classifier must explain.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's Hive Cell tips (20 pts each) and per-ball points show up as score increments on the FTC broadcast overlay. Each increment is a constraint: the detector should produce at least one Hive-entry candidate near that timestamp. Per-robot attribution still needs the identity model, but the alliance-level count is a hard check on total entries found (currently 1 of many).
findings.evidence: Detection of score changes in sport videos using textual overlays (ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/252052751_Detection_of_score_changes_in_sport_videos_using_textual_overlays): reports score-change detection rate 1.00, clock detection rate 0.852, and 4 false score-change declarations on its test material. Abstract/snippet only; full text not opened.

findings.method: Scoreboard localization before OCR (fixed ROI from first frames, or SIFT matching to a template, then OCR only the crop). Cropping is what makes OCR reliable on small overlay digits.
