findings.how_it_applies: The FTC overlay is static, so a fixed ROI calibrated once per video is enough. Crop, upscale, and binarize before reading; discard frames where the overlay is absent (replays, transitions) rather than letting them break the score timeline.
findings.evidence: Localization and Recognition of the Scoreboard in Sports Video Based on SIFT Point Matching (Guo et al., ResearchGate https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220989039_Localization_and_Recognition_of_the_Scoreboard_in_Sports_Video_Based_on_SIFT_Point_Matching): SIFT locates the scoreboard, then a simple neural-net digit classifier reads digits, with a higher recognition rate than a general-purpose OCR engine. Also an Electronic Letters on Computer Vision and Image Analysis 20(1):99-116, 2021 paper (https://elcvia.cvc.uab.cat/article/download/v20-n1-guntuboina/589/4064): YOLO finds the scoreboard, crop then OCR, reported near 100% OCR accuracy after cropping.

findings.method: Template-free digit reading with coarse-to-fine layout and temporal rules: detect the score region, recognize digits without per-font training, and use score-change rules and temporal correlation across frames to reject OCR noise.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout does not need a font-trained digit model. Temporal voting over a window of frames plus a rule that the score only increases (and only by plausible increments, e.g. 2 pts per ball, 20 per tip) filters single-frame misreads before they become false event labels.
findings.evidence: A Real-Time Score Detection and Recognition Approach for Broadcast Basketball Video (Miao, Zhu et al., ResearchGate https://www.researchgate.net/publication/221262832_A_Real-Time_Score_Detection_and_Recognition_Approach_for_Broadcast_Basketball_Video; Semantic Scholar https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/A-Real-Time-Score-Detection-and-Recognition-for-Miao-Zhu/7715fa09907c9c3ccce266b30aceee36dc2510c3). Abstract-level only.

findings.method: OCR-guided segment selection: OCR the scoreboard every N frames (paper samples at 0.1 s), validate read strings against regex formats, and when a counter increments, extract the corresponding segment for the detector. This turns OCR into a candidate generator and narrows the search window.
findings.how_it_applies: For Robo Scout, sample the overlay (e.g. every 0.1-0.5 s), and for each validated increment open a window around the timestamp to search for launches and Hive-entry frames, including the trajectory-reconstruction failure mid-air. Use the window to relabel/augment weak training data from the ~20 labeled videos.
findings.evidence: Automated Wicket-Taking Delivery Segmentation and Trajectory-Based Dismissal-Zone Analysis in Cricket Videos Using OCR-Guided YOLOv8 (arXiv 2510.18405, https://arxiv.org/html/2510.18405v2): samples frames at 0.1 s, ROI on scorecard, grayscale + power transform (gamma 7) + 15x15 dilation/erosion + median blur, regex validation, increment triggers segment extraction. Caveats from the paper: no OCR accuracy reported and no evaluation that the selected segments contain the events; the YOLO results do not feed back to validate OCR.

findings.method: Rule-based event decisions from overlay text changes (caption/score changes mapped to event rules), plus overlay absence (scoreboard shown only during live play) used to filter replays.
findings.how_it_applies: Use the overlay as a gate: count only during live-play frames where the overlay is visible, and treat score changes as the authoritative event count. Replays of a Hive tip should be deduplicated against the live event, not counted twice.
findings.evidence: A Survey on Content-Aware Video Analysis for Sports (arXiv 1703.01170, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.01170): describes rule-based event decisions from caption changes in baseball. Identification of replay segments patents (USPTO 7474698, https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/7474698): scoreboard usually appears only during live play, which can help detect replays.

findings.method: Open-source OCR building blocks for digit overlays: Tesseract (used in open scoreboard-ocr projects, e.g. https://github.com/Sunandagokhe/scoreboard-ocr and a basketball-highlights pipeline arXiv 1606.08955 that OCRs score, period and game clock to align play-by-play to video) and PaddleOCR PP-OCR (DB detection + CRNN recognition, current main README lists PP-OCRv6 with digital-display improvements, https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR). Note: the search snippets for PaddleOCR versions were inconsistent; verify against the repo before depending on a version.
findings.how_it_applies: For a 7-segment-like or bitmap FTC scoreboard with few glyphs, a small CNN digit classifier trained on crops from the ~20 labeled videos (auto-labeled by the score-increment rule) is likely more reliable than general OCR. Tesseract or PaddleOCR are good baselines for the validation oracle, not the only option.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/Sunandagokhe/scoreboard-ocr ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1606.08955 (Tesseract on score/clock overlay, abstract-level; full-text fetch returned unreadable PDF); https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR

recommendation: Build a scoreboard oracle for Robo Scout: fixed-ROI crop of the FTC overlay, sampled every 0.1-0.5 s, read by a small digit CNN (bootstrapped from Tesseract/PaddleOCR on the ~20 labeled videos), validated with regex and monotonic-increment rules, and temporal voting across frames. Use each validated score increment as a hard constraint: the alliance's Hive-entry and shot candidates must explain every increment in a window around its timestamp, and missing candidates trigger a search of that window with relaxed trajectory filters. Per-robot attribution still comes from the identity model; the overlay constrains totals, not who scored. Caveat: none of the sources reports accuracy on FTC-style overlays; the cited accuracy figures come from other sports and from abstracts only, so the oracle's precision must be measured on the labeled videos before use.

topic: Semi-automatic video annotation for ball and robot tracks (CVAT, Label Studio video, SAM 2 propagation, interpolation) for labeling every shot and Hive Cell entry across 20 matches

findings.method: SAM 2 promptable video segmentation with memory-based propagation
findings.how_it_applies: Click a robot or ball once on a keyframe and propagate the mask/track through the clip, with corrections on any frame. Good for robot identity tracks (robots are large), so human labels only need to be placed where the tracker drifts or swaps identity. For a ~10 px ball it is weaker: mask propagation is overkill, and a point prompt plus a physics fit is likely more reliable.
findings.evidence: SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos, Ravi et al., arXiv:2408.00714 (ICLR 2025 oral), https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00714 . Reports 3x fewer interactions for video segmentation and a model-in-the-loop data engine 8.4x faster at comparable quality, code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything-2

findings.method: CVAT SAM 2 tracker as an annotation action (keyframe then track forward)
findings.how_it_applies: Convert visible polygons on a frame into tracks and run tracking to a chosen frame. Supports polygons and masks but NOT rectangles, so it does not fit the current YOLO box pipeline directly. The on-prem path needs a Nuclio function plus Redis; the AI agent path requires CVAT 2.42.0 or later, and it loses active tracks on restart and allows one agent per tracking function. Budget for these operational limits before committing 20 matches to it.
findings.evidence: CVAT docs, Segment Anything 2 Tracker: https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/annotation/auto-annotation/segment-anything-2-tracker/ and https://docs.cvat.ai/docs/enterprise/segment-anything-2-tracker ; CVAT blog on SAM 2 video annotation: https://www.cvat.ai/blog/video-annotation-sam-2 . The blog and docs disagree on which plans get access, so verify the plan and version.

findings.method: Keyframe interpolation (linear) with dense keyframes, Label Studio video object detector / VideoVector tag
findings.how_it_applies: Label Studio interpolates bounding box position and size linearly between keyframes, and VideoVector interpolates polygon vertices linearly. Linear interpolation is wrong for ballistic ball flight, so keyframes must be dense around each launch or fit a parabola per flight segment. Its export with --interpolate-key-frames and sequence JSON can feed the existing Python pipeline. Good for robot boxes between sparse keyframes, not for ball arcs.
findings.evidence: Label Studio video object detector template: https://labelstud.io/templates/video_object_detector ; VideoVector tag: https://docs.humansignal.com/tags/videovector ; Label Studio 1.6 blog: https://labelstud.io/blog/label-studio-1-6-video-object-tracking-and-new-annotation-ui ; Label Studio SAM 2 tracking blog: https://labelstud.io/blog/video-object-segmentation-and-tracking-with-videovector-tag-for-sam-2-in-label-studio

findings.method: Event-level labeling instead of per-frame labeling (launch frame, entry frame, robot id, outcome per shot)
findings.how_it_applies: The scoring targets are per-robot shots and Hive Cell entries, so the cheapest ground truth is one row per launch: launch timestamp, robot ID, entry timestamp or none, and the tipping event. Per-frame boxes are only needed for training the detector. Interpolation tools are for geometry, and the event list is what evaluation needs. This cuts 20-match labeling to a few minutes per match and avoids over-labeling.
findings.evidence: Inferred from the task requirements (per-robot shot and entry counts) and the interpolation semantics in the Label Studio and Encord docs above. Encord separates interpolation (between existing labels) from object tracking (SAM 2 on consecutive frames): https://docs.encord.com/docs/annotate-interpolation . Not a published benchmark; treat as a design recommendation.

findings.method: Tracker-in-the-loop pre-labeling with human correction only on disagreements
findings.how_it_applies: Run the current YOLO ball detector and robot tracker over each match to propose tracks, then have the reviewer fix only flagged frames (ID swaps, missed launches, missed entries). Published FMO work built ground truth this way: label the first frame, run a tracker, then correct. Reviewers judged that corrections were needed on long sequences because small errors accumulate.
findings.evidence: Benchmarking EfficientTAM on FMO datasets, arXiv:2509.06536, https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06536v1 (TbD ground truth made by labeling first frame, running tracker, correcting; EfficientTAM TIoU 0.7093 on Falling Object, 0.4546 on TbD). Labellerr SAM 2 docs also recommend human review for long sequences: https://docs.labellerr.com/features/sam-2-object-tracking (product guide, not an evaluation).

findings.method: Stationary-camera semi-automatic annotation pipeline for small flying objects (shuttlecock)
findings.how_it_applies: A closely related setup: fixed camera, tiny fast object, semi-automatic labeling at scale (20,510 frames, 11 backgrounds, difficulty tiers). It reports a fine-tuned YOLOv8 at F1 0.86 in similar environments and 0.70 in unseen ones, which suggests holding out whole matches or venues when evaluating the Robo Scout detector. Note the title is 'One-Shot Badminton Shuttle Detection for Mobile Robots'. The fetched abstract did not say whether SAM 2 was used, so read the full text before copying its pipeline.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2603.06691, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06691 (v2 abstract, fetched)

findings.method: Benchmarks of SAM 2-family trackers on fast-moving and small objects
findings.how_it_applies: Before relying on SAM 2 propagation for balls, check how it performs on fast small objects. Reported results say DAM4SAM and SAMURAI perform well on harder fast-motion sequences, and the TSFMO benchmark covers 26 sports categories of small fast objects with 20 trackers. Use these to choose a tracker for ball and robot pre-labels rather than assume SAM 2 is best.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2512.09633, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.09633.pdf ; TSFMO benchmark, arXiv:2209.04284, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.04284

recommendation: Do not hand-label every frame of 20 matches. Build event-level ground truth (one row per launch with robot ID, launch time, entry time or none, and tip events), and pre-label it with the existing YOLO ball detector and robot tracker. Have a reviewer correct only the flagged frames: ID swaps, missed launches, and missed entries. Use SAM 2 (via CVAT's SAM 2 tracker or direct SAM 2 propagation) only for robot identity tracks, where objects are large. For the ~10 px balls, use point prompts with a parabolic fit between launch and apex, not linear keyframe interpolation. Verify the SAM 2 tracker benchmarks on small fast balls (arXiv:2512.09633) before adopting it for balls. Source gap: I found no published study that applies SAM 2 keyframe propagation to tiny, fast robotics balls, so the ball pipeline needs a pilot on 2 or 3 matches to measure it.

topic: SAM 2 / SAM 2.1 video tracking for following specific robots through occlusion and distractors; Apple Silicon speed; box prompts plus re-prompting

findings.method: SAM 2.1 promptable video segmentation with streaming memory (memory attention conditions each frame on past frames, predictions and prompts)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's SAM 2.1 seed-mask step can be extended from a single seed into a per-robot track: seed each selected robot from its identity-confirmed box, propagate the mask through the clip, and use the mask (not only the box) to keep per-robot ownership of nearby launches. The paper reports video accuracy gains with 3x fewer interactions than prior approaches, so re-prompting should be rare.
findings.evidence: SAM 2 paper, arXiv 2408.00714 (ICLR 2025 oral), https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00714 ; search-snippet summaries only, full PDF not opened

findings.method: SAM 2.1 official checkpoint speed table (tiny 91.2 FPS, small 84.8, base+ 64.1, large 39.5)
findings.how_it_applies: These FPS numbers were measured on an NVIDIA A100 (torch 2.5.1, CUDA 12.4), not on Apple Silicon, so they do not predict Mac speed. Plan on the tiny or small checkpoint for per-frame propagation on MPS and budget with a local benchmark on the 1280x720 clip before committing to every-frame tracking.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sam2 (fetched; table and 'Speed measured on an A100' note). Apple Silicon/MPS is not mentioned in that repo page.

findings.method: Anecdotal MPS timing and MLX port
findings.how_it_applies: Unverified third-party numbers: a blog reports SAM 2.1 Tiny via Ultralytics on PyTorch MPS at about 1.6 s for one point segmentation and about 1.5 s per multi-point update. A community MLX port (mlx-sam) reports a self-reported 1.27x speedup for the large model on one prompted 1024x1024 frame on an M2 Max; its quantized checkpoints mainly save memory, not latency. Together these suggest MPS per-frame SAM 2 may be too slow for every frame of a full match, so run it on keyframes or crops around the robot only. I found no independent MPS video-tracking benchmark.
findings.evidence: https://ice-ice-bear.github.io/posts/2026-04-08-sam2-mac (blog, not verified); https://pypi.org/project/mlx-sam/0.2.0/ (self-reported); https://docs.ultralytics.com/models/sam2 (surfaced in search, not fetched)

findings.method: DAM4SAM / SAM2.1++: distractor-aware memory plus introspection-based memory update, added to SAM2.1 without retraining
findings.how_it_applies: Directly targets the failure mode of robots being swapped with similar-looking distractors. Memory-based trackers, including SAM 2, struggle with distractors; DAM4SAM adds a distractor-aware memory and a DiDi distractor-distilled dataset. It is a candidate drop-in replacement for the plain SAM 2.1 tracker used for robot identity. Its abstract claims SOTA on six of seven benchmarks, but the page gives no numeric gains, so benchmark it on the labeled matches.
findings.evidence: Videnovic, Lukezic, Kristan, arXiv 2411.17576, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17576 ; code https://github.com/jovanavidenovic/DAM4SAM

findings.method: SAMURAI: motion-aware memory selection on SAM 2 with no retraining, real-time claim
findings.how_it_applies: Addresses SAM 2's fixed-window memory, which can propagate errors across frames during crowding and self-occlusion, which is exactly the robot-swap case in a crowded arena. Motion cues can also help predict where a robot is when a ball or another robot occludes it. Reported gains: +7.1% AUC on LaSOT_ext and +3.5% AO on GOT-10k. These are generic single-object benchmarks, not robot-specific; the paper page does not list a code repo, only the project page.
findings.evidence: Yang et al., arXiv 2411.11922, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11922 ; project page https://yangchris11.github.io/samurai/

findings.method: SAM2MOT / SAM2-Animal-Tracking: detector boxes as SAM 2 prompts, with re-prompting of existing tracks only on spatially unambiguous detections
findings.how_it_applies: This is the box-prompt-plus-re-prompt pattern Robo Scout needs. The robot YOLO detector supplies boxes; a track is re-prompted only when its detection is unambiguous (a key rule for not handing identity to the wrong robot when two similar robots overlap). Cross-object interaction is used to handle occlusion. Robo Scout's per-team identity classifier can serve as the gate that decides whether a re-prompt is allowed.
findings.evidence: SAM2MOT, arXiv 2504.04519, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.04519 , code https://github.com/TripleJoy/SAM2MOT ; SAM2-Animal-Tracking code https://github.com/ecker-lab/SAM2-Animal-Tracking (search snippets, not fetched)

findings.method: SAM-PD: iterative box propagation (previous-frame mask box becomes next-frame prompt) with jittered and scaled box prompts, keeping the candidate with the highest semantic similarity
findings.how_it_applies: Gives a concrete recipe for re-prompting without a detector on every frame: propagate the robot box from the last mask, jitter it to recover from drift, and select the candidate by appearance similarity to the identity reference. Useful as a fallback when the robot detector misses frames.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/infZhou/SAM-PD (search snippet only, not fetched)

findings.method: Limitation for balls (inference, not sourced)
findings.how_it_applies: SAM 2 is built for object masks in video, and Pollen balls are about 10 px. I found no source that tests SAM 2 on objects this small or this fast. Keep SAM 2 on the robots and use it for balls only if a local test shows it works; the ball-trajectory gap likely needs a different fix, such as the detector at 960 px with Kalman or motion-aware association.
findings.evidence: Inference from the SAM 2 paper scope and the task's ball size; no direct source

recommendation: Replace the single-seed SAM 2.1 use with a per-robot tracker: seed each robot from its identity-confirmed YOLO box, then propagate with SAM 2.1 tiny or small on MPS, and re-prompt a track only when the box is unambiguous and the team-identity classifier agrees (SAM2MOT / SAM2-Animal-Tracking rule). Benchmark DAM4SAM and SAMURAI as drop-in trackers against plain SAM 2.1 on the ~20 labeled matches, using robot-swap rate and per-robot shot attribution as the metrics. Measure MPS FPS locally on the 1280x720 clip first, since no source gives an Apple Silicon video-tracking number. Do not expect SAM 2 to fix ball loss, because the sources cover object masks, not 10 px balls.

topic: Field homography and camera calibration for a fixed side-view sports camera (image to field coordinates, robot position and ball flight constraints, known field markers)

findings.method: Planar homography from known pitch model with line-extremity correspondences and RANSAC, then decomposition into camera intrinsics and extrinsics (SoccerNet calibration baseline)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's camera is fixed, so one calibration per video (or per venue setup) is enough. Mark field-model points (mat edges, tape line intersections, goal/Cell footprints) in a few frames, fit H with RANSAC, decompose to camera parameters, and reuse for every frame. This maps each robot's floor contact point to field coordinates so identity can be gated by position continuity and zone rules. Caveat: a plain homography only holds for points on the floor plane. Hive Cell rim points sit above the floor, so use the decomposed camera (PnP) for them, not H alone.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/SoccerNet/sn-calibration (official SoccerNet calibration repo: RANSAC homography, ellipse/line refinement, decomposition into camera parameters). Baseline description also in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.06006 (SoccerNet 2023 challenge results).

findings.method: Keypoint detector plus homography (YOLO-style pose/keypoint model on pitch landmarks, cv2.findHomography on whatever subset is visible)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout already runs YOLO. A YOLO keypoint model trained on FTC field landmarks (mat corners, Cell corners, goal corners, tape intersections) can replace hand calibration. Because the number of visible landmarks varies, use findHomography with RANSAC and reject frames with too few inliers. This pattern is directly reproducible in Ultralytics plus OpenCV.
findings.evidence: https://blog.roboflow.com/camera-calibration-sports-computer-vision/ (Roboflow tutorial: trains YOLOv8 keypoints on pitch landmarks, computes homography with OpenCV findHomography because visible keypoint count changes with camera motion).

findings.method: Keypoint-and-line joint optimization with one generalizing model (PnLCalib)
findings.how_it_applies: Most relevant if the broadcast view or camera setup varies across held-out matches. PnLCalib refines the camera using both detected keypoints and line extremities in a non-linear optimization, and the authors report one model covering the SoccerNet distribution rather than one per camera location. For Robo Scout the field geometry is fixed, so the benefit is robustness to partial occlusion by robots and the Cell rather than generalization.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08401 (PnLCalib: Sports Field Registration via Points and Lines Optimization); https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08401 ; open implementation lineage in the SoccerNet challenge page https://nikolasent.github.io/deeplearning/computervision/calibration/competitions/2023/06/20/SoccerNet-Camera-Calibration-2023.html

findings.method: Dense keypoint set (line-line intersections, line-conic intersections, conic tangent points) with HRNet heatmaps and PnP refinement (2023 SoccerNet top solution)
findings.how_it_applies: Shows that adding many derived keypoints from intersections and tangent points, then refining with PnP, gives stable calibration with fewer manual labels. Analogue for FTC: derive extra keypoints from mat-edge intersections and the Cell's rectangular rim so calibration survives when the Cell is partly occluded.
findings.evidence: https://nikolasent.github.io/deeplearning/computervision/calibration/competitions/2023/06/20/SoccerNet-Camera-Calibration-2023.html (top-1 write-up: 57 keypoints, HRNetV2-w48 heatmaps, PnP solver).

findings.method: Single-model keypoint and line calibration with a shared solver and reported accuracy (sportcal)
findings.how_it_applies: Open-source reference for a calibration pipeline with a web app for checking projections. The repo's model is for hockey, soccer, tennis and basketball, so it is not directly usable for FTC, but its label format and reprojection-error check (reported 7.7 px on hand labels) are a template for validating Robo Scout calibration against hand-labeled frames.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/oscardiaz1331/sportcal

findings.method: Single-camera 3D ball lift using gravity dynamics and court geometry, with a cost function that avoids model drift
findings.how_it_applies: Addresses the lost-mid-air problem. Once the camera is calibrated, each 2D ball track can be lifted to 3D by fitting a gravity model with drag-free ballistic dynamics, constrained by known launch zones. Robo Scout can then test whether the 3D trajectory crosses the Cell rim plane inside the Cell footprint, which is more reliable than 2D overlap. The 2015 ISCSS paper reports that earlier monocular reconstruction suffers from model drift and proposes a new cost function to fix it. The 2012 IEEE paper integrates court specifications and ball physics for the 2D-to-3D inference.
findings.evidence: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6115930/ (3D ball trajectory reconstruction from single-camera sports video, volleyball/court geometry); http://www.shenlj.cn/en/Shen_CP2M_iscss2015.pdf (gravity-model fitting with new cost function); https://arxiv.org/html/2506.07981 (real-time soccer ball localization from a single camera).

findings.method: Parabola-only fitting is fragile; use physics priors with tolerance for deflection
findings.how_it_applies: Per the 2025 soccer ball paper summary found in search (not verified against the full text), real paths rarely follow a simple parabola because of deflections and mis-hits, so a pure parabola fit will reject real Hive entries. Robo Scout should fit a ballistic model with a robust loss (e.g., RANSAC over segments) and allow a contact or deflection breakpoint, rather than requiring one clean parabola per flight.
findings.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.07981 (the search summary attributes this parabola critique to the 2025 soccer paper; confirm by reading the paper before relying on it).

recommendation: Calibrate the fixed camera once per setup: label FTC field landmarks (mat corners, tape intersections, Cell rim corners) on a few frames, fit the camera with RANSAC PnP (not a plain floor homography, because the Cell rim is elevated), and validate by reprojection error on held-out frames. Use the calibrated camera to (1) map each robot's floor contact point to field coordinates for identity gating by position continuity and zone rules, and (2) lift each ball track to 3D with a robust ballistic fit, then count a Hive entry only if the 3D path crosses the Cell rim plane inside the Cell footprint. No FTC-specific calibration source was found; the SoccerNet, PnLCalib, Roboflow and sportcal sources are the closest references and must be adapted to the FTC field model.

topic: Event-level evaluation methodology: time-tolerance matching, per-entity precision/recall, held-out benchmarks across matches

findings.method: Time-tolerance event matching with one-to-one assignment (SoccerNet action spotting protocol)
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout should score each predicted launch or Hive-entry as a true positive only if it falls within a tolerance delta of a ground-truth event of the same type, with each prediction and each ground-truth event used at most once. Unmatched predictions are FP and unmatched ground truth is FN. Report results at several deltas (e.g., 0.5s, 1s, 2s) rather than one, because the Hive-entry timing is fuzzy when balls rise into the cell from below. Robo Scout's ball paths are lost mid-air, so tolerance sweeps show whether misses are timing errors or true misses.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet original paper, https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.04527 (abstract: spotting = finding event anchors; tolerance delta from 5 to 60 s; Average-mAP baseline 49.7%). Full-text read via ar5iv https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1804.04527: a prediction is a TP if within delta of a ground-truth anchor; per-class AP per delta; mAP averaged over classes; Average-mAP is the area under the mAP-vs-delta curve. The paper does not explicitly state one-to-one matching or the same-class rule; these are implied by the per-class evaluation. SoccerNet 2023 results describe Average-mAP as area under the mAP curve over tolerances (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.06006). The tight version uses 1-5 s tolerances (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.09951).

findings.method: Per-entity identity-level precision/recall (IDF1 / IDP / IDR)
findings.how_it_applies: To attribute shots to the correct robot, compute identity-level TP/FP/FN by a global one-to-one matching between predicted robot tracks and ground-truth robot tracks, then report IDP, IDR and IDF1. This directly measures the identity-swap problem: a shot credited to the wrong robot counts as an IDFP plus an IDFN, not a free pass. Use the same matching to produce per-robot shot precision and recall.
findings.evidence: Ristani et al., Performance Measures and a Data Set for Multi-Target, Multi-Camera Tracking, ECCV 2016, https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01775 (abstract confirms a pair of precision-recall measures that treat all error types uniformly and emphasize correct identification). IDF1 = 2*IDTP/(2*IDTP+IDFP+IDFN) as summarized in secondary sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.13457. The IDF1 formula details could not be read from the PDF in this session; verify exact definitions in the original paper.

findings.method: Report HOTA with DetA/AssA decomposition alongside IDF1 and ID switches
findings.how_it_applies: Separate detection quality (DetA: TP/(TP+FN+FP)) from association quality (AssA: Jaccard over trajectory-level TPA/FNA/FPA). This tells Robo Scout whether shot misses come from the ball detector (low DetA) or from robot identity tracking (low AssA). Also count identity switches per robot, since the current failures are swaps. Use the TrackEval/HOTA reference implementation for computation.
findings.evidence: Luiten et al., HOTA: A Higher Order Metric for Evaluating Multi-object Tracking, IJCV 2021, arXiv:2009.07736. Full-text read via ar5iv https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2009.07736: DetA = TP/(TP+FN+FP); AssA = mean over TPs of TPA/(TPA+FNA+FPA); HOTA_alpha = sqrt(DetA*AssA); final HOTA averages alpha over 0.05 to 0.95 in 0.05 steps. The paper states MOTA overweights detection and IDF1 overweights association. Reference code: https://github.com/JonathonLuiten/HOTA-metrics (named in search results, not fetched).

findings.method: Event-level matching for sparse rare events: avoid metrics dominated by single events
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout has few Hive entries per match, so a single missed entry can swing AP. Report raw TP/FP/FN counts and per-match counts alongside any AP-style score, and include bootstrap confidence intervals over matches rather than over events.
findings.evidence: Deep Learning for Sports Video Event Detection survey, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.03991 (notes strict tolerance windows make the task much harder and that rare classes can be dropped because the metric is highly sensitive to single predictions). Secondary; verify against the survey text.

findings.method: Held-out benchmark split at the match level (no leakage across matches or halves)
findings.how_it_applies: Split Robo Scout's ~20 labeled videos by whole match, never by frame or launch window, so windows from the same match never appear in both train and test. Keep a sealed test set of matches not used for threshold or classifier tuning, mirroring the SoccerNet challenge set whose labels are withheld and scored only through a server. With 20 videos, use leave-matches-out cross-validation and report variance across folds.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet-v2 splits are made per match with two halves per match; the challenge split labels are withheld and scored via an evaluation server (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13367v1.pdf, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.07846). A ball-header paper explicitly splits at game level to avoid train/test window overlap (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.39300). The SoccerNet leakage rationale was not explicitly confirmed in the sources read.

recommendation: Adopt a two-level evaluation for Robo Scout: (1) event-level matching of predicted launches and Hive entries to ground truth using a same-type time tolerance with one-to-one assignment, reported across a sweep of tolerances (e.g., 0.5 to 2 s) so timing error is separated from true misses; (2) entity-level scoring of per-robot shots using a global one-to-one identity matching that yields IDP/IDR/IDF1 and identity switch counts, with HOTA's DetA/AssA as a diagnostic split. Build the held-out benchmark by splitting the ~20 labeled matches at the match level, with a sealed test set and leave-matches-out cross-validation, reporting per-match counts and confidence intervals. Verify the exact IDF1 and HOTA formulas in the original papers and TrackEval before implementing, since the PDF text could not be extracted in this session.

topic: Active learning and human-in-the-loop correction loops for video event detectors (prioritizing uncertain clips, model-assisted labeling, retraining cadence), applied to Robo Scout

findings.method: Entropy-based clip selection for review with max-pooled frame scores (uncertainty sampling beats random at low budgets)
findings.how_it_applies: Score each candidate launch/shot window by entropy of the current shot classifier (or detector class confidences), pool per-frame scores to clip level with max pooling, and send the top-scoring clips to human review instead of random clips. Robo Scout's per-launch reviews on ~20 videos can be used to measure whether entropy ranking finds more mislabeled shots than random sampling.
findings.evidence: Giancola et al., 'Towards Active Learning for Action Spotting in Association Football Videos', CVPRW 2023, https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2304.04220 (fetched). Reported: Entropy Measure reached 90% of final performance with ~16% of data vs ~45% for random sampling on SoccerNet-v2 with NetVLAD++; max pooling beat mean pooling for clip scores. Note: the Uncertainty Measure gave only limited gains on the denser dataset.

findings.method: Adaptive review batch sizes with continual fine-tuning instead of retraining from scratch each round
findings.how_it_applies: Start with small review batches and grow them as labeled data accumulates (e.g. 2%, then 5%, then 10% of the pool), and fine-tune the existing model for a few epochs per round at a fixed learning rate rather than training from scratch. This cuts the number of retrain cycles and wall-clock time on the MPS machine, which matters for YOLO retraining on Apple Silicon.
findings.evidence: Giancola et al. CVPRW 2023, https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2304.04220 (fetched). Adaptive schedule reduced rounds from ~100 to ~30 and saved ~70% of time; continual fine-tuning (20-epoch bootstrap, then 5 epochs per round) kept the uncertainty advantage over random sampling.

findings.method: Margin-based uncertainty for detectors with per-image aggregation and class-balancing weight for rare classes
findings.how_it_applies: For each detection compute the top-1 vs top-2 class score margin, convert to an uncertainty (1-gap)^2, aggregate per image by sum, and add a weight to boost underrepresented predicted classes. Applicable to YOLO detections of balls (Pollen vs Nectar confusion) and robot-identity classifier outputs. Batches are formed by splitting the unlabeled pool into fixed groups and annotating the highest-scoring group.
findings.evidence: Brust et al., 'Active Learning for Deep Object Detection', https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1809.09875 (fetched; the PDF link was not readable). Reported on new VOC classes with class weighting: ~24.3 mAP after 250 samples vs 21.9 for random; gap narrows at full data (32.7 vs 32.4).

findings.method: Localization-aware and hybrid uncertainty/diversity selection for detectors
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's ball detector misses small Pollen balls mid-air; selecting frames where box localization is unstable (IoU between intermediate and final box) or where detections disagree across frames targets exactly those hard cases, rather than only confident-classification errors.
findings.evidence: Search-snippet only, not fetched: Kao et al. 'Localization-Aware Active Learning for Object Detection' (arXiv 2018), cited in https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11960984; Wu et al. arXiv 2204.07965 (instance-level uncertainty + diversity), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.07965. Treat as unverified details.

findings.method: Binary or frame-level human queries on the model's least-certain moment, then retrain per round
findings.how_it_applies: Instead of asking annotators to label whole clips, ask a narrow question (e.g. did this ball enter the Cell? which robot launched it?) at the single frame where the model is least certain. This makes review faster for the shot-entry decisions that the current pipeline gets wrong.
findings.evidence: Ji et al., 'Are Binary Annotations Sufficient? Video Moment Retrieval via Hierarchical Uncertainty-Based Active Learning', CVPR 2023, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023/papers/Ji_Are_Binary_Annotations_Sufficient_Video_Moment_Retrieval_via_Hierarchical_Uncertainty-Based_CVPR_2023_paper.pdf (search snippet only, not fetched).

findings.method: Pre-label, correct, review-sample, retrain loop with edit-rate monitoring and cold-start bootstrap
findings.how_it_applies: Hand-label a small seed set (guidance in the Ultralytics material suggests 100-200 examples per new class), train a rough v0 model, have it pre-label new frames, let annotators correct only the wrong boxes, and track the per-batch edit rate. A rising edit rate signals drift from the labeled distribution and triggers retraining. Reviewing every pre-label before it enters a training version guards against baking systematic model errors into ground truth.
findings.evidence: Ultralytics glossary and academy material, https://www.ultralytics.com/glossary/data-labeling and https://academy.ultralytics.com/courses/build-with-ultralytics-platform/auto-annotation (search snippets only, not fetched). Academic analogue: arXiv 2504.01010 (iterative YOLO loop from a small manual seed set), https://pdf.arxiv.org/pdf/2504.01010 (snippet only). Blog note that proposals are worst on occluded/rare cases is from https://www.ultralytics.com/blog/auto-labeling-active-learning-tools (snippet only).

findings.method: Temporal boundary-focused clip-budgeted labeling
findings.how_it_applies: For event timing (launch and Cell-entry instants), rank clips by MC-dropout uncertainty and request labels only at predicted event boundaries. Relevant to the problem that ball paths are lost mid-air, since boundary frames are where tracker handoffs fail.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2604.15173, 'Boundary-Centric Clip-Budgeted Active Learning for Temporal Action Segmentation', https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.15173 (search snippet only, not fetched).

recommendation: Build a review queue that ranks candidate launch and Cell-entry windows by the shot classifier's entropy (max-pooled over frames), start with small review batches of about 2% of the pool, and grow them to 5% then 10% as labels accumulate. Fine-tune the existing YOLO and classifier weights for a few epochs per round rather than retraining from scratch, and check the ranking against random sampling on the ~20 labeled matches. Ask narrow binary questions (ball entered Cell? which robot launched?) at the least-certain frame. Pre-label with the current detector and track the per-batch correction rate as a drift signal. Note that the Brust and Giancola numbers come from other domains (VOC, SoccerNet), and the Ji, Kao, and Ultralytics details were taken from search snippets and not read in full.

topic: Occlusion by a container frame/net and confirming a ball settled inside a basket from a side view (settle, stop, persist; persistence and color-count methods)

findings.method: Occlusion-aware temporal ball detection (TOTNet): use a short clip (3D conv over several frames) so the detector infers a ball's position when it is hidden, trained with occlusion augmentation and a visibility-weighted loss.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout loses balls mid-air and when they pass behind the Cell frame. A temporal model over a window of frames, or per-frame detections fused with a motion model, can carry a ball through partial and full occlusion instead of dropping the track. Reported gains on occluded frames: accuracy 0.63 to 0.80, RMSE 37.30 to 7.19 (table tennis, tennis, badminton; the paper's own TTA dataset). Transfer to a 10 px ball is unverified.
findings.evidence: TOTNet: Occlusion-Aware Temporal Tracking for Robust Ball Detection in Sports Videos, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09650 (abstract/HTML at https://arxiv.org/html/2508.09650v1)

findings.method: Low-confidence detections kept for association (ByteTrack): match low-score boxes to existing tracklets by overlap/motion instead of discarding them, which recovers objects that are partly occluded.
findings.how_it_applies: Balls behind the net or frame often produce low-confidence or no YOLO detections. Keeping low-score ball boxes and associating them to a predicted ball track (rather than starting new tracks) addresses the 'ball path lost mid-air' failure. Use the same mechanism to keep per-robot tracks alive through brief occlusion, which may also reduce identity swaps.
findings.evidence: ByteTrack: Multi-Object Tracking by Associating Every Detection Box, Zhang et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06864 (reports IDF1 gains of 1 to 10 points across nine trackers)

findings.method: Stopped-object detection via dual or multi-rate background models (dual-background subtraction with different learning rates; multi-detector with absorption rates per motion class and a finite state machine that labels moving / short-term stationary / long-term stationary).
findings.how_it_applies: A ball that settles inside the Cell stops moving and would be absorbed into a background model, so pure frame-difference would lose it. Keeping a slow-adapting background model alongside a fast one lets a settled ball stay flagged as a stationary foreground blob for longer. The state machine maps directly to ball states: in-flight, settled, persisting. Caveat: the PubMed record (PMID 28026761) could not be fetched; its title and details are from search snippets only and should be checked before citing.
findings.evidence: Search summaries pointing to a dual-background stationary-object paper (Springer, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1155/2011/858502) and a three-detector state-machine paper (PMID 28026761, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28026761/, not verified in full). Survey of comparative methods: Bayona et al., AVSS 2009, https://repositorio.uam.es/bitstream/handle/10486/667138/comparative_bayona_AVSS_2009_ps2.pdf

findings.method: Offline gap filling after tracking: Gaussian-smoothed interpolation (GSI) or linear interpolation between track endpoints, applied after the forward pass, with an explicit note that GSI did not beat linear interpolation on MOT17-val (OC-SORT).
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's ball paths break mid-air. Running a post-hoc pass that fills gaps between the last and next confident ball detections (linear for short gaps, smoothed for longer) restores full trajectories for the shot classifier. Test linear vs GSI on the 20 labeled videos, since the sources disagree on which is better.
findings.evidence: StrongSORT: Make DeepSORT Great Again, https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13514 (introduces GSI); Observation-Centric SORT, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14360 (finds GSI worse than linear on MOT17-val)

findings.method: Lost-track association via motion over appearance: a Kalman-style motion model alone can associate across long occlusions, while appearance re-ID features are unreliable under severe occlusion and cause identity switches.
findings.how_it_applies: Supports the decision to use motion-based association for balls and for robot tracks through occlusion, and warns against leaning on the per-team identity classifier when robots overlap or occlude. Identity recovery should prefer motion and position continuity over appearance.
findings.evidence: ByteTrack, https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06864; DeepSORT/SORT comparison summarized in Deep Learning-Based Multi-Object Tracking survey, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.13457

recommendation: Replace the single-frame ball detection with a ByteTrack-style tracker that keeps low-confidence ball boxes and carries tracks through occlusion on a motion model, then add an offline gap-fill pass (linear first, GSI as a comparison) so each shot yields a complete trajectory. Detect settling with a slow-adapting background model or a per-blob stationarity state (moving / settled / persisting) inside the Cell region, and count only balls that persist there for N frames. No source found covered a ball settling in a net or a color-count method, so those parts still need the team's own labeled-video validation.

topic: Lightweight end-to-end architectures for per-player stat extraction from sports video (detection -> tracking -> event -> attribution)

findings.method: Decouple per-player identity from detection: run a person detector plus a tracker (StrongSORT in the SoccerNet-GSR baseline, DeepSORT in the 2024 winner), with appearance re-ID embeddings used to keep tracklets consistent. Identity is a tracklet-level property, not a per-frame one.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's robot identity swaps between similar robots are a re-ID/tracklet-consistency problem. Add an appearance embedding per robot box (team color, number plate, or a re-ID model trained on robot crops) and associate with appearance plus motion, instead of relying on the frame-level classifier alone.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet GSR baseline, Somers et al., arXiv 2404.11335 (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.11335v1): YOLOv8 person detection, StrongSORT with PRTreID embeddings. Winner, Golovkin et al., arXiv 2504.06357 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06357): YOLOv5m detector, DeepSORT with re-ID.

findings.method: Tracklet-level majority voting for identity attributes: predict role/team/jersey per detection, then take the most common label within each tracklet, and cluster tracklet-averaged embeddings (K-means into 2 teams) for team assignment.
findings.how_it_applies: Instead of classifying each frame's robot identity, aggregate the per-team/per-robot classifier outputs over each track and assign identity by vote (and by averaged embedding clustering for alliance). This directly reduces the 87% per-frame roster error and stops a single wrong frame from flipping attribution. Note the paper does not specify tie or null handling, so define it yourself.
findings.evidence: Golovkin et al. arXiv 2504.06357 (abstract: majority voting within tracklets is mentioned in the SoccerNet 2025 results report arXiv 2508.19182); SoccerNet-GSR baseline arXiv 2404.11335 section on aggregation over time (role and jersey by majority vote, team by K-means over averaged PRTreID embeddings of player tracklets).

findings.method: Evaluate with an attribute-aware HOTA-style metric: similarity = localization similarity x identity similarity, where identity similarity requires all attributes (role, team, jersey) to match. This separates detection/localization errors from attribution errors.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout needs per-robot shot attribution scored separately from shot detection. Adopt a GS-HOTA-like score for the robot-identity track and a per-robot counting error for shots and Hive entries, so you can see which stage is the bottleneck on the held-out match.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet-GSR paper arXiv 2404.11335: GS-HOTA = HOTA with Sim = LocSim x IdSim, tau = 5 m, matches over alpha in [0.05, 0.95]; baseline 22.26% test GS-HOTA. Module oracle ablation: bounding-box detection is the weakest stage (35.28) and jersey number is 56.75, suggesting the identity stage is where a pipeline most often fails.

findings.method: Stage-wise oracle ablation to find the bottleneck: replace one module with ground truth and measure the metric change.
findings.how_it_applies: Use the same approach on Robo Scout: swap in ground-truth robot IDs, then ground-truth ball tracks, then ground-truth Cell entries, and see which swap recovers the most stat accuracy. This is a cheap way to prioritize work among the detector, tracker, launch scanner and classifier.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet-GSR arXiv 2404.11335 module ablation (team side 92.00, ReID 87.42, calibration 51.39, pitch 49.99, jersey number 56.75, bbox detection 35.28).

findings.method: Dedicated lightweight tracker for tiny, fast objects: TrackNetV2 uses a multi-frame heatmap CNN for shuttlecock/ball tracking, reported as 2.6 FPS to 31.8 FPS speedup, with 85.2% accuracy and 97.2% precision on a new match.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's yellow Pollen balls are about 10 px and get lost mid-air. A TrackNet-style model that takes stacked consecutive frames (and outputs a ball heatmap) is designed for exactly this small-fast-ball regime, and can be used for trajectory continuity rather than per-frame YOLO detection. Caveat: the citation attribution is inconsistent (Sun et al. 2020 vs. Huang et al. 2019 in RacketVision), so check the paper front matter; TrackNetV4 reports different numbers for TrackNetV2, and one table-tennis comparison found YOLOv4 beat TrackNetv2 on some ball-speed datasets, so benchmark both on your data.
findings.evidence: TrackNetV2 summary via Papers with Code (https://astro.paperswithcode.com/paper/tracknetv2-efficient-shuttlecock-tracking); TrackNetV4 arXiv 2409.14543 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.14543); RacketVision arXiv 2511.17045 (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17045v3); badminton all-deep system arXiv 2308.12645 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12645).

findings.method: Event-level structure: the racket-sport and basketball stat repos typically detect the ball, detect the player, then fire a shot/event from trajectory features (trajectory curve fit to make/miss, in basketball shot repos chonyy/basketball-shot-detection and anishcd/basketball-shot-detection) and link events to the nearest or most active player by spatial proximity.
findings.how_it_applies: Robo Scout's Hive-entry problem (only 1 of many found because trajectories break mid-air) can be handled by fitting a smooth parametric trajectory (e.g. a parabola in image space) through gap-tolerant ball detections, then deciding entry by intersection with the Cell box, instead of requiring continuous tracks. This is the pattern in the basketball make/miss repos, adapted to rising balls.
findings.evidence: chonyy/basketball-shot-detection (https://www.github.com/chonyy/basketball-shot-detection): trajectory curve fit to ball detections, make/miss color coding. anishcd/basketball-shot-detection (https://github.com/anishcd/basketball-shot-detection). nitinhemaraj/Basketball-shot-detection (YOLOv8 based; README claims 97% shot detection accuracy, unverified).

findings.method: Tracking-by-detection with ByteTrack for lightweight multi-object tracking, with a thesis benchmark on basketball: ByteTrack beat BoT-SORT with MOTA 0.876 and IDF1 0.937 at 43.77 ms per frame using YOLOv8.
findings.how_it_applies: Swap or compare the tracker against your current setup for the robot track layer. ByteTrack keeps low-confidence boxes in association, which can help when robots occlude each other briefly. Pair with appearance re-ID for similar robots, because IDF1 measures exactly the identity swaps you are seeing.
findings.evidence: UGM thesis on basketball player tracking, etd.repository.ugm.ac.id (https://etd.repository.ugm.ac.id/home/detail_pencarian_downloadfiles/1666472); the search summary also cites a Hugging Face racquet-sports-analyzer using YOLO11n-pose with ByteTrack (unverified, no model card metadata).

findings.method: Camera calibration / homography from image to court plane, so per-robot position is checked in court coordinates rather than pixel boxes. The baseline maps each box bottom to the ground plane via a homography and scores in pitch space.
findings.how_it_applies: For a fixed camera, a one-time homography to the field or Cell plane lets you test which robot is near a launch or Hive entry using physical distance. This is a cheap way to reduce cross-robot credit errors because the nearest robot in court coordinates is a stronger attribution cue than image overlap.
findings.evidence: SoccerNet-GSR baseline arXiv 2404.11335 (pitch localization with TVCalib, homography from bounding box bottom to pitch); winner arXiv 2504.06357 (SegFormer-based camera parameter estimation).

recommendation: Fix identity and attribution first, as tracklet-level pipelines do: (1) add an appearance re-ID embedding per robot and associate with StrongSORT/ByteTrack-style tracking, (2) replace per-frame identity labels with majority voting inside each robot tracklet (plus embedding clustering for alliance), (3) score with an attribute-aware GS-HOTA-style metric and run oracle ablations to find the bottleneck, and (4) for ball and Hive entries, fit smooth trajectories through gapped detections (or try a TrackNetV2-style multi-frame heatmap model for the 10 px Pollen balls) and decide entry by intersection with the Cell region. Sources: arXiv 2404.11335, arXiv 2504.06357, TrackNetV2 via Papers with Code, arXiv 2409.14543.

topic: code audit: shots and entries

findings.method: Origin gate: a trail only becomes a shot if the ball is inside the tracked robot's upper-body box within 0.17 s before its first sample. Any trail that starts after the ball has left the box, or where the box is missing, is rejected.
findings.how_it_applies: Missed shots. Fragments that begin mid-flight (after a dropout or occlusion) can never pass, and a None robot box at that time is silently skipped, so the shot is dropped with no error.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:116-127 (_source, delay loop, containment test at 125), 119-120 (None box continues), 40-52 (RobotBoxes.at returns None for gaps >0.22 s or >0.06 s past the end)

findings.method: Trail termination on dropout: a trail is retired when no blob is seen for max(0.075, 2.25/fps) s, and every trail is also retired after 1.3 s from its first observation. At 60 fps the dropout limit is about 4.5 frames.
findings.how_it_applies: Flights that pass behind the Cell rim or get missed for a few frames are split or truncated. The orphaned pieces then fail the origin gate in finding 1, so the whole shot is lost. Long lobs over 1.3 s are cut the same way.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:320 (stale_after), 343 (alive test with 1.3 s cap), 346-348 (retire-and-attribute only when stale)

findings.method: Camera-cut and large-motion frames clear every active trail without evaluating it. Only trails retired at line 346 or at end-of-video (361-364) are passed to attributed().
findings.how_it_applies: Any in-flight shot that overlaps a broadcast cut, pan, replay or overlay animation (more than 28% of pixels changing) is discarded silently. This is a direct missed-shot path that is easy to fix.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:350-353 (active = [] with no attributed call), 346 and 361-364 (the only emission points)

findings.method: Blob gating is absolute and motion-based. The residual test requires mean motion >=8 and 23% of ball pixels with diff >13. A global gate skips blob detection entirely when fewer than 9 pixels changed. Frames are downscaled to 960 wide, and the scale switches to 1536 when config.robots is non-empty.
findings.how_it_applies: The apex and the slow approach to the opening are the lowest-motion phases, so they are the ones most likely to fail. A 10 px Pollen ball at 960 px is about 7 px. The same video yields different detections depending on whether robots are configured, so results are not stable across configs.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:64-73 (size, area, aspect and residual gates), 71-72 (residual motion test), 354 (whole-frame gate), 288-289 (960 vs 1536 scale switch), 339 (INTER_AREA resize)

findings.method: Rise and velocity gates reject real launches. Initial upward velocity must exceed 0.18*height. The rise must be at least max(0.028*height, 1.6 diameter) and must reach 0.02*height above the robot top. The upward run stops on any +0.012*height jitter and is capped at 0.65 s.
findings.how_it_applies: Low or lobbed shots, shots whose apex is hidden by the robot body, and shots with one noisy frame in the rise are rejected or truncated. Truncation also feeds the classifier a shorter sample (see finding 14).
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:146-149 (velocity gate), 158-162 (upward run; 159 for the 0.65 s cap and 0.012*height jitter stop), 165-167 (rise and lowest_y rules)

findings.method: A shot classifier hard-filters launches before they are counted or matched to Hive entries. The floor is 0.4, and the code comment says it removed 1 of 20 real shots on one held-out match.
findings.how_it_applies: Each launch the classifier rejects is never emitted as a shot. Its Hive entry is also lost, because verified_candidates only sees the launches that survived the filter. The loss is about 5% of real shots on that match, and the threshold rests on one match.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:16-18 (load and filter before event creation), 979 (verified_candidates receives the filtered launches); backend/shot_model.py:53-55 (SHOT_FLOOR and the 1-of-20 note), 58-64 (likely_shot)

findings.method: Attribution uses a margin test on source_error. Two candidates within 0.16 of each other cause the shot to be dropped, not reassigned. source_error is the box-centre offset in box widths plus 1.5 times the back-projection delay, so it favours centre proximity and a late delay, not the true launcher.
findings.how_it_applies: When two alliance robots' boxes both contain the launch origin, which is common in a cluster, the shot is missed. When the margin passes, the chosen robot is the one whose centre is closest, which is not necessarily the one that fired.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:294-303 (attributed, margin test at 303), 180-183 (source_error formula)

findings.method: Identity errors feed straight into the origin test. Each team's box is taken from frame["robots"][team], and the identity model is about 87% accurate. RobotBoxes.at interpolates across consecutive frames whenever the centres move less than max(30, 1.25 box width).
findings.how_it_applies: After an identity swap between two nearby, similar robots, the swapped box is within the continuity gate, so the interpolated box blends the two robots. A launch from robot B then passes team A's origin test and is credited to A. This matches the reported swaps.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:34-38 (per-team box selection; missing team yields None), 44-49 (interpolation and continuity gate at 47-48)

findings.method: Attribution ownership during merging and dedupe. Cross-team stitching lets the earlier fragment keep its team and absorbs later fragments from another team. Dedupe keeps the highest-confidence candidate, not the one whose origin fits best.
findings.how_it_applies: The team credited to a merged or deduplicated shot is set by timing and confidence, not by geometry. A correct fragment from the right robot can be discarded in favour of a wrong-robot fragment with higher confidence.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:202-203 (cross-team window 0.42 s), 216-223 (cross-team merge), 227-230 (prior team kept), 242 (dedupe sorted by confidence only)

findings.method: Duplicate tolerance is narrower than one frame. Two samples match only if dt < 0.016 s, but at 60 fps the frame period is 0.01667 s. The time window also uses the back-projected launch time, which varies with delay by up to 0.17 s.
findings.how_it_applies: A ball tracked in two fragments with a one-frame offset never counts as a duplicate, so the same shot is counted twice. Two candidates for the same shot can also fall outside the 0.17 s window and survive.
findings.evidence: backend/launches.py:253 (dt < 0.016 test), 246 (0.17 s time window), 177 and 116 (back-projected time varies with delay)

findings.method: Hive mouth scan only detects Pollen. Detection is YOLO filtered to the pollen class, with a yellow-only colour fallback, and verified_candidates skips every non-pollen launch.
findings.how_it_applies: Red and blue Nectar entries are structurally impossible to find, so every Nectar entry is missing from the output regardless of tracking quality. This is a large, direct cause of finding only one entry.
findings.evidence: backend/hive_entries.py:81 (yellow-only HSV range), 134 and 157 (classes=pollen), 243 (launch["kind"] != "pollen" skip)

findings.method: Hive arrival geometry is strict and brittle. arrival() needs a downward crossing of the lip with at least 0.16*height of prior rise, and rejects any single later sample outside the x-range or below the box. settled_entry() needs an unbroken inside run, and the run ends at the first sample outside. Tracks are finalized after 0.18 s without a detection.
findings.how_it_applies: A rising entry in this low side view fails the descent test (line 26). A single stray detection or a rim occlusion of more than 0.18 s splits or kills the track, so the entry is never found. At 30 Hz sampling (stride 2 at 60 fps), about 4 to 6 samples per transit are available to meet the 0.13 to 0.18 s rest requirements.
findings.evidence: backend/hive_entries.py:24-26 (descent and prior-rise rule), 29 (any out-of-box sample rejects), 32-36 (settle window), 58-62 (unbroken inside run), 194 (0.18 s track gap), 126 and 149 (rate 30 Hz)

findings.method: Projected linking has a time bug. projected_quality compares the extrapolated x against the Cell entry x at hit.time, but it only extrapolates for min(gap, 0.27) seconds. Gaps up to 0.84 s are allowed.
findings.how_it_applies: For any gap longer than 0.27 s, the projection is evaluated at the wrong time and is compared against the wrong x, so a correct match is rejected. This is a deterministic cause of missed Hive links for the slow shots that most need linking. Constant horizontal velocity means the projection should use the full gap.
findings.evidence: backend/hive_entries.py:219 (gap window .03 to .84 s), 221 (x taken at hit.time), 223 (projected = last + v*min(gap, .27)), 224-225 (error tolerance .038)

findings.method: Exact overlap relies on two time bases. The mouth scan timestamps are index/fps, while the launch tracker uses decoded pts. Exact overlap needs samples within 0.063 s of each other.
findings.how_it_applies: If pts and index/fps drift by more than about one frame (variable-rate or screen recordings, seek offsets), exact overlap fails and matching falls back to the projected path, which only accepts single-team matches. This is plausible but not verified against the video's timestamps.
findings.evidence: backend/hive_entries.py:177 (index/fps), 208 (gap <= .063); backend/launches.py:327-332 (pts and fallback time)

findings.method: Duplicate and ambiguous Hive matches. One physical ball can yield two finds when its track is split (find_arrivals finalizes the track after a 0.18 s gap, and both halves can qualify). The second find can then project-match a different same-team launch. Ties within a team are accepted without a margin check, and earlier finds claim launches first.
findings.how_it_applies: A phantom Hive entry can be credited to a shot that did not enter. Tie acceptance can pick an arbitrary launch. This is plausible and not verified on the labeled videos.
findings.evidence: backend/hive_entries.py:194-201 (split tracks, finds from finished and active tracks), 240 (earliest find first), 249-253 (projected and exact selection, same-team acceptance at 253)

findings.method: Silent gating upstream of Hive matching. Hive scanning is disabled when camera_motion is set. Each alliance needs exactly one marked cell, otherwise it is skipped. A failed mouth scan only logs a warning and falls back to launch paths. The entry time window is 0.18 to 1.55 s from the back-projected launch time.
findings.how_it_applies: Entries are missing for whole matches or alliances without any error in the results, and shots whose flight takes longer than 1.55 s, or is shorter than 0.18 s, cannot link.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:2 (camera_motion gate), 4-6 (exactly one cell mark), 34-38 (warning fallback), backend/hive_entries.py:243-244 (0.18 to 1.55 s window)

findings.method: The shot classifier scores only the upward run, with raw count features. Its inputs come from launch["samples"], which stops at the apex. Features such as len(time) and duration depend on the detection sampling rate, and the loader returns None silently on a bad file.
findings.how_it_applies: Scores depend on frame rate and on where the rise ends, not on the full flight, so a shot that reaches the Cell can look like a non-shot. Load failures disable the classifier with no signal. This is plausible and needs a check against the training data.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:18 and 24 (scores and stores launch["samples"]), backend/launches.py:184-187 (samples = upward run), backend/shot_model.py:26 (raw count features), 46-50 (silent None on error)

recommendation: Make the launch tracker survive occlusion and cuts before changing any scoring: in backend/launches.py, call attributed() on trails before clearing them at the camera-cut reset (lines 352-353), and allow dropout gaps of about 0.2 to 0.25 s with motion-predicted continuation instead of the 0.075 s stale limit (line 320). Then fix the projection time bug at backend/hive_entries.py:223 and add Nectar colors to the mouth scan (lines 81, 134, 157, 243). This is one change to the tracker plus two targeted fixes, and each should be validated against the ~20 labeled videos, since I did not run the pipeline.

topic: code audit: robot tracking

findings.method: Team tracks choose detections independently, with no global assignment
findings.how_it_applies: analyze() calls tracking.advance() for each team in roster order, all against the same `robots` list (vision.py:873, built at 831-841). Each TeamTrack picks its own best box (reidentify 244-288, recognize 299-326, named 361-368). Nothing prevents two teams from locking the same physical robot, and nothing assigns one detection per team. Earlier teams in dict order get first pick. The collision check at vision.py:878-884 only reverts the later state and sets the box to None. It does not decide which team is correct. scipy linear_sum_assignment is already imported (vision.py:10) but is not used for team-to-detection matching.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:862-885, 873, 878-884; scipy import at backend/vision.py:10

findings.method: Appearance signature is color-only and cannot separate same-alliance robots
findings.how_it_applies: signature() builds HSV histograms with 18x3x3 bins over the top and bottom halves of the box (vision.py:44-56). It carries no shape, texture, number, or position information. Same-alliance robots share the same team color, so similarity() (105-108) is nearly equal for both. The Identity gallery (111-141) and reidentify scoring (iou + similarity - distance penalty, 274-278) then decide on overlap and position alone, and the .08 margin (279) collapses to ties near crossings. AppearanceRecovery's hue tint (backend/robot_recovery.py:22-60, _tint at 76-80) has the same blind spot.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:44-56 (signature), 105-108 (similarity), 111-141 (Identity), 274-281 (scoring and margin); backend/robot_recovery.py:22-60, 76-80

findings.method: Position-only gating widens over time and then falls back to appearance alone
findings.how_it_applies: In reidentify, reach = side*(.6+.15*min(since_verified,20)) (vision.py:255-256) grows to about 3.6 robot widths. plausible() accepts any box within that reach (259-262). After since_verified > 30 (268) the whole candidate set is accepted, and Identity.choose decides on appearance alone with minimum .62 (269-271). Same-color rivals pass that threshold, so a dropout longer than 30 samples can reacquire the wrong robot.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:252-272

findings.method: The named-detection path skips all spatial and classifier gating and jumps the track
findings.how_it_applies: When the main detector emits a robot_<team> class (targets[team], built at 777 and 833-841), reidentify is skipped entirely because of `if generic and not named` (vision.py:356). Then `max(named, ...)` is accepted at confidence >= .48, or >= .30 with agreement (361-365), with no plausible() or prior-distance check. On accept, the RobotTrack and nano tracker are rebuilt on that box (368-370). A single misclassified box from the team-class detector therefore becomes a full identity jump.

findings.method: The identity classifier is bypassed in the common path and only gates the rare path
findings.how_it_applies: TeamTrack.classify is assigned at vision.py:867 but is consumed only inside reidentify -> recognize (263-264). reidentify runs only when there is no named detection (356). recognize() accepts a classifier-confident box only if top >= .7 and margin >= .3, and only if it is near the track or persists for 3 samples (311-320). Otherwise its fallback ranks nearby boxes by iou + 1.5*p with a p >= .05 cutoff (321-322). That cutoff is near zero, and the 1.5 weight lets a geometrically closer rival with low team probability beat the true robot. The classifier never acts as a hard veto. The recognize() docstring claims a robot the classifier rules out is never followed, but the code does not enforce that.

findings.method: Classifier is silently absent in several cases
findings.how_it_applies: Identity classifiers are built only if the separate robot.pt detector loaded (vision.py:757-758 and the block through 766). A StopIteration from the shared model is swallowed (`except StopIteration: pass`, 766-767). If no identity-<team>.pt exists and identity.pt lacks the team, the track falls back to the color-only path with no warning. has_identity_model/identity warnings (778-781) do not cover this case. Callers therefore cannot tell from the output whether identity correction ran.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:757-767, 777-781

findings.method: Per-team binary classifier and renormalization limits
findings.how_it_applies: Per-team models are two-class (team vs other), built in TeamClassifier (71-87). Their probability for a robot is computed with no context from the alliance partner. The shared model renormalizes over rivals only for teams the model knows (83-87, 96-101). Because roster teams the model does not know are silently dropped from `rivals`, the probability can be inflated for a rival with an unseen class. The classifier also runs only on crops of boxes with no temporal smoothing beyond the 3-sample rule in recognize.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:71-101, 311-320

findings.method: Snap and template fallbacks are identity-agnostic
findings.how_it_applies: RobotTrack.advance replaces the estimate with a 70/30 blend toward the highest-IoU detection of any robot (vision.py:186-190), with no identity check. It falls back to grayscale TM_CCOEFF_NORMED template matching over the padded search window with threshold .69 (192-199). A same-shape rival inside the window matches, and the color signature is not consulted. These are the main routes by which the feature track follows the rival during overlap.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:168-212 (snap 186-190, template 192-199)

findings.method: Identity gallery learns from detections that may already be wrong
findings.how_it_applies: Identity.confirm adds the chosen box to a rolling gallery of 8 (vision.py:128-131). reidentify calls confirm when agreements % 10 == 0 and similarity to the seed >= .5 (286-287). The .5 threshold is loose for same-color robots, and the sample is the box chosen by the same possibly-wrong logic. This creates a feedback loop: a swap teaches the gallery the rival's appearance, which then reinforces the swap. The seed is permanent, but the rolling gallery is not anchored to it.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:111-141, 286-287

findings.method: Collision rollback restores only part of the track state
findings.how_it_applies: Before advancing, analyze() snapshots (copy(tracker), supported) per team (vision.py:871-872). On a collision (IoU > .50 at 878-881) it restores only tracker and supported (882-884) and sets the box to None. Not restored: the nano tracker (mutated in place by nano.update at 333), the AppearanceRecovery state, identity gallery updates from reidentify (286-287), recognize's pending counter (313-320), since_verified, agreements, and identity_frames. The next frame therefore starts from a partly corrupted state, and the same ambiguity recurs.

findings.method: Nano tracker is re-seeded from whatever box was selected
findings.how_it_applies: follow() calls reset_nano(best) whenever the box is not already the robot (vision.py:290-294). Named acceptance and recovery do the same (368-370, 352), and nano_box() tracks appearance only (330-345). Once a wrong box is selected, the nano template is rebuilt from the rival, so the appearance tracker reinforces the swap instead of correcting it.

findings.method: Detector outputs are merged without de-duplication
findings.how_it_applies: robot.pt detections are appended to the generic robots list (vision.py:831-834). The main model's 'robot' class is appended too (840-841). There is no NMS or cross-detector dedupe. The same physical robot can appear twice with near-identical boxes, which makes reidentify's len(candidates)==1 shortcut (270s) and the margin tests (279, 396 region) unreliable. Duplicates also push the scoring toward the held-box fallback (276-281).
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:831-841, 265-281

findings.method: Refinement is appearance-only and resolves collisions by deleting boxes
findings.how_it_applies: track_refinement.track_direction seeds one TrackerNano per team from human anchors (track_refinement.py:34-61). It uses no identity classifier and no exclusivity between teams. refine_roster nulls a team box when it overlaps another team box > .49, except on anchor frames (refine_roster lines 112-118), instead of reassigning it. merge_box (69-88) either averages forward and backward hits when overlap >= .26 or picks the closer-in-time hit (< .8 s), so a swap in one direction is blended or dropped. The refined robots feed match_tracks and shot attribution, because the per-frame loop skips match_tracks when refine is True (vision.py:887-888 and 920-927).
findings.evidence: backend/track_refinement.py:34-61, 69-88, 91-121; backend/vision.py:700, 887, 920-927

findings.method: Refinement is disabled for camera-motion matches
findings.how_it_applies: refine requires nano_params, anchors, and not camera_motion (vision.py:700). On moving-camera matches the bidirectional correction never runs, and the forward tracker's swaps are final. The identity logic above is then the only defense.
findings.evidence: backend/vision.py:700

recommendation: Replace the independent per-team choices with one per-frame assignment: build a team-by-detection cost matrix from the TeamClassifier probability, IoU to the last trusted box, and appearance similarity, then solve it with the already-imported linear_sum_assignment. Make the classifier a hard veto on every path, including the named-detection branch (vision.py:361-371) and the lost-track branch. Roll back the full per-team state (nano, recovery, gallery, pending) on collision instead of only tracker and supported (vision.py:870-885), and stop folding unverified detections into the identity gallery (vision.py:286-287).
